messages.subject: knmodels with LCAR prior
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I was studying the knmodels() function, and wonder if it can accomodate LCAR prior for spatial random effect, instead of 'bym2'?  My intention is to include an unstructured spatial random effect in the model. Since LCAR has both structured and unstructured effects, I thought it may be appropriate. So I had a go with editing the example given as:

res <- inla.knmodels(y ~ f(time, model='rw1') + # model = 'rw1', 'rw2', 'ar1',
                       f(space, model='generic1', Matrix = Q.Leroux, constr =. TRUE),
                     data=dat, family='poisson', E=dat$e, progress=TRUE,
                     control.st <http://control.st>=list(time=time, space=space,
                                     spacetime=spacetime, graph=graph, type=4), #c(1, 2, 3, 4)
                     control.compute=list(dic=TRUE, waic=TRUE, cpo=TRUE))

I am not sure with this, if the appropriate constraints can be established.
Many thanks for clarifications.
Aminath

messages.body_plain:
Currently, it will add the constraints (as if the main effect has rank deficiency). I've updated the code so will (try to) check before adding it (it will be in the next testing version).
If you want to do it yourself you can use something like

y ~ f(time, model = 'rw1') +
  f(space, model = 'besagproper2', graph = "graph.file") + ## I prefer "besagproper" instead (has interpretability)
  f(spacetime, model = 'generic0',
    Cmatrix = kronecker(R.t, R.s),
    extraconstr = list(A = constr.t, e = rep(0, n.s))

P.S: I've some (old) code at http://www.leg.ufpr.br/~elias/cursos/br2015/ (check r/cwb-example.R) for models including the Knorr-Held ones.

best regards,
Elias

messages.subject: Formula including quadratic terms
messages.body_plain:
Hi R-INLA community,

I am constructing a species niche model where I included two covariates. I included a quadratic term for both of them. My (very practical) question is: do these quadratic terms need to be formulated in a separate variable (example 1), or is it okay to formulate them with "^2" (example 2)? I don't know how the output will look like in both cases (and the running of the model on the cluster takes 12 days ;) )

example 1)
f = y ~ -1 + Intercept + sanddynamics + sanddynamics_quadratic + springtide + springtide_quadratic +  f(w, model = spde, group = w.group, control.group = list(model = "ar1"))

example 2)
f = y ~ -1 + Intercept + sanddynamics + sanddynamics^2 + springtide + springtide^2 +
  f(w, model = spde, group = w.group, control.group = list(model = "ar1"))

Thank you!

Charlotte

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Formula including quadratic terms
messages.body_plain:
Dear Charlotte,

(A + B + C) ^  2 is shorthand for all main effects and their two way interactions (A + B + C + A:B + A:C + B:C)
Use I() when you want to transform a variable. E.g. I(A^2)

I would recommend using poly(A, 2) instead of A + I(A^2). poly() generates orthogonal variables whereas A + I(A^2) might lead to highly correlated variables.
Another option is to center A to a sensible point within its range and scale it by multiplying it by some power of 10. The result should be a variable with a range that somewhat resembles c(-1, 1). Squaring a variable with 0 somewhere in the middle of the range is less likely to be highly correlated than squaring a variable with 0 outside of the range of the data. Scaling ensures that the squared covariates don't get very large or very small.

You might want to try it on a small dataset before running it on the cluster.

Best regards,

Thierry

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Formula including quadratic terms
messages.body_plain:
Dear Charlotte,

Please keep the mailing list in cc. Others might benefit from the conversation.

Yes. y ~ -1 + Intercept + poly(sanddynamics, 2) + poly(springtide, 2) +
  f(w, model = spde, group = w.group, control.group = list(model = "ar1")) should work.

Note that poly() has one downside IMHO: the resulting coefficients are harder to interpret. That is why I prefer to center and scale with meaningful values.

messages.subject: spatiotemporal model validation and forecasting
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am seeking after some help with model validation and forecasting from spatiotemporal models (this is my first attempt doing this using R-Inla, I am relatively new to INLA and still exploring it)

I have been trying to do these with some example data given in https://github.com/aritz-adin/Identifiability_Constraints_article/blob/main/R/CARmodels_INLA.R
This is early data of Breast cancer mortality risk. So the model concerns estimating relative risk using Expected counts.

My intention is to first validate the model using last 4 years data and forecast for next 2 years.  In the attached code I have prepared data frames for model validation (set NA for observed counts in last 4 years)  and forecasting (set NA for both observed and expected counts in the next 2 years). The model is Poison GLM with random effects Knorr-Held (2000) Type 4.

I am not sure about the followings and would appreciate some help:
1. Do. the expected counts in the validation set also needs to be set as NA?
2. The model for relative risk requires an expected count (E), but as the forecast dataset would not ideally have these, Eoes not including the E part in the inla() function makes sense? I mean is it really estimating relative risk if excluded? If not  how do I included expected counts in the forecast set?
2. I would like to compute RMSE, MAE and Person correlation coefficient for the validation set. I understand that Model$summary.fitted.values give estimates  for the mean. But, how do I get estimates for the Observed values (i.e Y)? This is required to compute these discrepancy measures.

Many thanks for the help
Aminath

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] spatiotemporal model validation and forecasting
messages.body_plain:
Sorry for not being clear.

In the model
 y ~ Poisson(rE)
where y and E are given to model r. Setting E=NA inla will treat it as E=1. And inla does the computations for the inference for r (mean, mode, quantiles, and the full distribution if you ask). Given r, E is used to get y, considering the equation r = y/E.

E is a function of population (and gender and age specific rates, usually). Therefore you need population forecasts to compute E for the forecasting of y (of course, you estimate r instead of rate). Once you have E and r, E _computed_ from the population and r _predicted_ (you can use summaries or even apply the full distribution estimated) by your model, you can apply the equation aforementioned.

best regards,
Elias

Hi again,

I am sorry for posting my questions in the same topic, again. I had tried the version 24.04.25-1, but the problem does not go away. The vb.correction of the compact algorithm is still aborted, and the classic algorithm is still not comparable with the version before 2024. To make sure the issue is not due to the sloth data (https://www.paulamoraga.com/tutorial-point-patterns/), I did the same test for another two data sets,

* Solanum (https://www.paulamoraga.com/book-spatial/point-process-modeling.html)
* Gorillas (https://inlabru-org.github.io/inlabru/articles/2d_lgcp.html)

Also, the test was run on the following six INLA versions,

  * INLA 22.05.07 (stable): the default inla.mode is "classic", and inla.mode="experimental" is "compact" as the default of INLA version > 22.11.08.
  * INLA 23.09.09 (stable)
  * INLA 23.12.17 (testing)
  * INLA 24.01.07 (testing)
  * INLA 24.02.09 (stable)
  * INLA 24.04.25-1 (testing)

Including the version 22.05.07 is because its default inla.mode is "classic".

The model structure is just a combination of "intercept + random field".   The table below shows predictions.

I think the compact algorithm in INLA 22.05.07 gives nonsensible values because it was in an "experimental" mode. For the other INLA versions, the warning "vb.correction is aborted" still occurs in the model fitting for the three data sets. I guess the instability of the compact estimates is due to the unsuccess of vb.correction. It seems to me that the compact algorithm is very sensitive and "vb.correction is aborted" is unavoidable. The test results of the compact algorithm concern me. What strategies should I use to let the compact algorithm to give me reliable results?

For the classic algorithm, the predictions between the INLA versions before and after 2024 are dramatically different. In NEWS.md of INLA, no information about changes made to the classic algorithm. It is unclear why the classic algorithm performs so differently in the 2024 INLA versions. The untold changes worry me. Given that the classic has been used for quite a long time (from version 22.05.07 or even before), I reckon it is more robust than the compact. My question is why the 2024 classic performs so differently?

All the R code, results and log files of the test are in the attached zip file.

Best,
Wen-Hsi

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Differences in inference when using different algorithms and different versions of INLA
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Differences in inference when using different algorithms and different versions of INLA
messages.body_plain:
Hi

I looked over the example concentrating on 'gorilla'

These are examples of models where the posterior almost flat, hence details
matters.

Like priors: for models with little data, you _have_ to be informative with
priors. that is precisions

I changed to

            # P(sigma > 1) = 0.01
            prior.sigma = c(0.3, 0.01))

and added

           control.fixed = list(prec.intercept = 1),

constr=T for the spde will also do good.

the consequence of using non-informative priors is that internal correction
fail,

[1802] "        *** Please (re-)consider your model, priors, confounding, etc."
[1803] "        *** warning *** iterative process seems to diverge,
'vb.correction' is aborted"

these msg's is a clear sign that something is `not good'.

with the changes above, the compact mode runs without any issues and the DIC
values seems stable

btw, DIC values are notorious sensitive to small changes in the hyperparameters,
as its a sum, not a mean, hence you might tighten up the inner optimisation

            control.inla = list(tolerance.step = 1e-8),

or smaller.

Older versions of INLA was less good in these cases, and therefore the optimizer
was improved to handle better these situations. (in the fall of 2023 sometime)

Also, there was a bug in the compact mode VB correction for the mean, where the
prior for fixed effects was not properly added, which was fixed here

# INLA 24.02.09
* Fixed a bug: prior means was not accounted for, doing the VB mean correction

the classic model is no longer suppored in the sense that no changes are done on
that part of code beyond bug-fixing (if that happens).

The compact mode is way better, both wrt speed and accuracy

If there is anything else, please let us know

H

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] sum-to-zero constraint
messages.body_plain:
Hello

When using ar1 as a time effect, do the following models need to add additional constraints?
Do ID.year and ID.year1 need to add constr=TRUE?

Elias T. Krainski <eliask...@gmail.com> 于2024年3月7日周四 19:30写道：

> This fits (beta + beta_i + beta_t) X_it (although the indexing here is not very precise) and having constraints in both 'rw2' and 'besag' is fine. But this is not yet a spatio-temporal model for the regression coefficient, where you would have beta_it.
>
> On Thu, 7 Mar 2024 at 13:15, Reza Hajipour <rehaj...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > It's great. Thank you.
> >
> > Yes, I have both fixed slop and random slop covariates. In this case, as you mentioned, 'beta' and 'beta_i' interact, so we need the constraint.
> >
> > I am fitting a spatio-temporal model with varying coefficients (random slop) covariates. If we have evidence that covariates vary across regions over time, is the model as follows?
> >
> > formula <- O ~ X +
> > f(ID.area1, X, model="besag", graph=TR.adj, constr=T) +
> > f(ID.year1, X, model="rw2", constr=T) +
> > f(ID.area2, model="besag", graph=TR.adj, constr=T) +
> > f(ID.area3, model="iid", constr=F) +
> > f(ID.year2, model="rw2", constr=T) +
> > f(ID.year3, model="iid", constr=F)
> >
> > Is (beta + beta_i) X_it enough or we need (beta + beta_i + beta_t) X_it? I mean is f(ID.year1, X, model="rw2", constr=T) necessary or not?
> >
> > On Thursday 7 March 2024 at 11:38:12 UTC+3:30 Elias T. Krainski wrote:
> > >  For this case, you have to consider either having "+ X" or not. If you have it, the constraint is needed, otherwise not. This will lead to having either (beta + beta_i) X_i (where beta_i should be constrained) or just beta_i X_i.
> > >
> > > On Thu, 7 Mar 2024 at 10:23, Reza Hajipour <rehaj...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > Thank you so much. It was so helpful for me.
> > > >
> > > > As you explained and based on the articles I have studied, the models with improper joint distribution like ICAR, leading to an identifiability problem with the model intercept.
> > > >
> > > > My model also includes the spatial varying coefficient covariates (along with fixed effect intercept) as follow:
> > > >
> > > > formula <- O ~ X +   f(ID.area1, X, model="besag", graph=TR.adj, constr=T) +
> > > >   f(ID.area2, model="besag", graph=TR.adj, constr=T) +
> > > >   f(ID.area3, model="iid", constr=F)
> > > >
> > > > In this case, does the ICAR specification of covariate 'X' again lead to an identifiability problem with the model intercept (does it interact with the model intercept) and is the constraint necessary or not?
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > On Thursday 7 March 2024 at 09:59:30 UTC+3:30 Elias T. Krainski wrote:
> > > > >
> > > > > Hi,
> > > > >
> > > > > You do not always need constr = TRUE. It is not needed for 'iid' model, or any other model with proper joint distribution. But sometimes you want it, for example for the case of having a long range correlation that interacts with some other model component. You only need constraint in intrinsic models if another model component includes its null space.
> > > > >
> > > > > Please take a look at the example below, where I illustrate the fact that you do not always need to add a constraint while working with intrinsic models.
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > library(INLA)
> > > > >
> > > > > n <- 30
> > > > > x <- scale(cumsum(rnorm(n)))
> > > > >
> > > > > plot(x)
> > > > >
> > > > > y <- rpois(n, exp(2 + x))
> > > > >
> > > > > fit1 <- inla(
> > > > >     y ~ f(i, model = 'rw1'),
> > > > >     data = list(i = 1:n, y = y),
> > > > >     family = 'poisson'
> > > > > )
> > > > >
> > > > > ## The intercept captures the overall mean
> > > > > fit1$summary.fix
> > > > >
> > > > > ## posterior mean for the constrained random effect is around zero
> > > > > summary(fit1$summary.random$i$mean)
> > > > >
> > > > > ## Now, take the intercept ou of the linear predictor
> > > > > ## Then, the constraint in the random effect is no longer needed
> > > > > fit2 <- inla(
> > > > >     y ~ 0 + f(i, model = 'rw1', constr = FALSE),
> > > > >     data = list(i = 1:n, y = y),
> > > > >     family = 'poisson'
> > > > > )
> > > > >
> > > > > ## unconstrained random effect is around the intercept (not fitted separately)
> > > > > summary(fit2$summary.random$i$mean)
> > > > >
> > > > > ## However, the fitted values are similar (not exactly the same as the priors are different and there are some small numerical differences while doing the computations)
> > > > > summary(fit1$summary.fitted.values$mean)
> > > > > summary(fit2$summary.fitted.values$mean)
> > > > >
> > > > > regards,
> > > > > Elias
> > > > >
> > > > > On Thu, 7 Mar 2024 at 08:34, Reza Hajipour <rehaj...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > sum-to-zero constraints ensure the identifiability, if yes, is it necessary to have this constraint on 'iid' parts, as follows?
> > > > > >
> > > > > > formula <- O ~ X +
> > > > > >   f(ID.area, model="besag", graph=.... , constr=TRUE) +
> > > > > >   f(ID.area1, model="iid", constr=TRUE) +
> > > > > >   f(ID.year, model="rw2", constr=TRUE) +
> > > > > >   f(ID.year1, model="iid", constr=TRUE)
> > > > > >
> > > > > > As you mentioned the constr=TRUE is default, if I don't add it to f(...) parts of the above formula, the conster is True and the sum-to-zero constraint is done for all random effects?
> > > > > > On Saturday 2 March 2024 at 19:04:36 UTC+3:30 Helpdesk (Haavard Rue) wrote:
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > in this case the constr=T will only impose a constraint on the 'besag'
> > > > > > > part of the model, not the 'iid'
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > On Sat, 2024-03-02 at 07:13 -0800, Reza Hajipour wrote:
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > Thank you.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > What about the "BYM" model where we have two random effects, one with
> > > > > > > > ICAR prior and one with gaussian prior, does it give sum-to-zero as
> > > > > > > > follows:
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > f(ID.area, model="BYM", graph=.... , constr=TRUE, rankdef=1)
> > > > > > > > On Saturday 2 March 2024 at 13:04:09 UTC+3:30 Helpdesk (Haavard Rue)
> > > > > > > > wrote:
> > > > > > > > > yes, this gives a sum-to-zero constraint. for the besag and rw1 I
> > > > > > > > > would
> > > > > > > > > also add scale.model=TRUE
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > for 'besag' and 'rw1' which are intrinsice, then constr=TRUE is
> > > > > > > > > default.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > you add more constraints with the argument 'extraconstr' if needed.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > On Fri, 2024-03-01 at 22:02 -0800, Reza Hajipour wrote:
> > > > > > > > > > Hello
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > I want to add a sum-to-zero constraint on the random effects of a
> > > > > > > > > > spatio-temporal model. Is it enough to put  constr=TRUE   as
> > > > > > > > > > follows:
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > formula <- O ~ X +
> > > > > > > > > >   f(ID.area, model="besag", graph=.... , constr=TRUE, rankdef=1) +
> > > > > > > > > >   f(ID.year, model="rw1", constr=TRUE, rankdef=1)

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] sum-to-zero constraint
messages.body_plain:
Hello

When using ar1 as a time effect, do the following models need to add additional constraints?
Do ID.year and ID.year1 need to add constr=TRUE?

st2<- O ~ 1+f(ID.city,model="bym",graph=g,scale.model = T,constr=T,hyper=pc1)+
  f(ID.year,model="ar1",hyper=pc2,constr=T)+
  f(ID.year1, model = "iid",hyper=pc2,constr=T)+
  f(ID.city1,model="iid",hyper=pc2,group=ID.year2,control.group = list(model="ar1"))

Elias T. Krainski <eliask...@gmail.com> 于2024年3月7日周四 19:30写道：

> This fits (beta + beta_i + beta_t) X_it (although the indexing here is not very precise) and having constraints in both 'rw2' and 'besag' is fine. But this is not yet a spatio-temporal model for the regression coefficient, where you would have beta_it.

>
> On Thu, 7 Mar 2024 at 13:15, Reza Hajipour <rehaj...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > It's great. Thank you.
> >
> > Yes, I have both fixed slop and random slop covariates. In this case, as you mentioned, 'beta' and 'beta_i' interact, so we need the constraint.
> >
> > I am fitting a spatio-temporal model with varying coefficients (random slop) covariates. If we have evidence that covariates vary across regions over time, is the model as follows?
> >
> > formula <- O ~ X +
> > f(ID.area1, X, model="besag", graph=TR.adj, constr=T) +
> > f(ID.year1, X, model="rw2", constr=T) +
> > f(ID.area2, model="besag", graph=TR.adj, constr=T) +
> > f(ID.area3, model="iid", constr=F) +
> > f(ID.year2, model="rw2", constr=T) +
> > f(ID.year3, model="iid", constr=F)
> >
> > Is (beta + beta_i) X_it enough or we need (beta + beta_i + beta_t) X_it? I mean is f(ID.year1, X, model="rw2", constr=T) necessary or not?
> >
> > On Thursday 7 March 2024 at 11:38:12 UTC+3:30 Elias T. Krainski wrote:
> > >  For this case, you have to consider either having "+ X" or not. If you have it, the constraint is needed, otherwise not. This will lead to having either (beta + beta_i) X_i (where beta_i should be constrained) or just beta_i X_i.
> > >
> > > On Thu, 7 Mar 2024 at 10:23, Reza Hajipour <rehaj...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > Thank you so much. It was so helpful for me.
> > > >
> > > > As you explained and based on the articles I have studied, the models with improper joint distribution like ICAR, leading to an identifiability problem with the model intercept.
> > > >
> > > > My model also includes the spatial varying coefficient covariates (along with fixed effect intercept) as follow:
> > > >
> > > > formula <- O ~ X +   f(ID.area1, X, model="besag", graph=TR.adj, constr=T) +
> > > >   f(ID.area2, model="besag", graph=TR.adj, constr=T) +
> > > >   f(ID.area3, model="iid", constr=F)
> > > >
> > > > In this case, does the ICAR specification of covariate 'X' again lead to an identifiability problem with the model intercept (does it interact with the model intercept) and is the constraint necessary or not?
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > On Thursday 7 March 2024 at 09:59:30 UTC+3:30 Elias T. Krainski wrote:
> > > > >
> > > > > Hi,
> > > > >
> > > > > You do not always need constr = TRUE. It is not needed for 'iid' model, or any other model with proper joint distribution. But sometimes you want it, for example for the case of having a long range correlation that interacts with some other model component. You only need constraint in intrinsic models if another model component includes its null space.
> > > > >
> > > > > Please take a look at the example below, where I illustrate the fact that you do not always need to add a constraint while working with intrinsic models.
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > library(INLA)
> > > > >
> > > > > n <- 30
> > > > > x <- scale(cumsum(rnorm(n)))
> > > > >
> > > > > plot(x)
> > > > >
> > > > > y <- rpois(n, exp(2 + x))
> > > > >
> > > > > fit1 <- inla(
> > > > >     y ~ f(i, model = 'rw1'),
> > > > >     data = list(i = 1:n, y = y),
> > > > >     family = 'poisson'
> > > > > )
> > > > >
> > > > > ## The intercept captures the overall mean
> > > > > fit1$summary.fix
> > > > >
> > > > > ## posterior mean for the constrained random effect is around zero
> > > > > summary(fit1$summary.random$i$mean)
> > > > >
> > > > > ## Now, take the intercept ou of the linear predictor
> > > > > ## Then, the constraint in the random effect is no longer needed
> > > > > fit2 <- inla(
> > > > >     y ~ 0 + f(i, model = 'rw1', constr = FALSE),
> > > > >     data = list(i = 1:n, y = y),
> > > > >     family = 'poisson'
> > > > > )
> > > > >
> > > > > ## unconstrained random effect is around the intercept (not fitted separately)
> > > > > summary(fit2$summary.random$i$mean)
> > > > >
> > > > > ## However, the fitted values are similar (not exactly the same as the priors are different and there are some small numerical differences while doing the computations)
> > > > > summary(fit1$summary.fitted.values$mean)
> > > > > summary(fit2$summary.fitted.values$mean)
> > > > >
> > > > > regards,
> > > > > Elias
> > > > >
> > > > > On Thu, 7 Mar 2024 at 08:34, Reza Hajipour <rehaj...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > sum-to-zero constraints ensure the identifiability, if yes, is it necessary to have this constraint on 'iid' parts, as follows?
> > > > > >
> > > > > > formula <- O ~ X +
> > > > > >   f(ID.area, model="besag", graph=.... , constr=TRUE) +
> > > > > >   f(ID.area1, model="iid", constr=TRUE) +
> > > > > >   f(ID.year, model="rw2", constr=TRUE) +
> > > > > >   f(ID.year1, model="iid", constr=TRUE)
> > > > > >
> > > > > > As you mentioned the constr=TRUE is default, if I don't add it to f(...) parts of the above formula, the conster is True and the sum-to-zero constraint is done for all random effects?
> > > > > > On Saturday 2 March 2024 at 19:04:36 UTC+3:30 Helpdesk (Haavard Rue) wrote:
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > in this case the constr=T will only impose a constraint on the 'besag'
> > > > > > > part of the model, not the 'iid'
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > On Sat, 2024-03-02 at 07:13 -0800, Reza Hajipour wrote:
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > Thank you.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > What about the "BYM" model where we have two random effects, one with
> > > > > > > > ICAR prior and one with gaussian prior, does it give sum-to-zero as
> > > > > > > > follows:
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > f(ID.area, model="BYM", graph=.... , constr=TRUE, rankdef=1)
> > > > > > > > On Saturday 2 March 2024 at 13:04:09 UTC+3:30 Helpdesk (Haavard Rue)
> > > > > > > > wrote:
> > > > > > > > > yes, this gives a sum-to-zero constraint. for the besag and rw1 I
> > > > > > > > > would
> > > > > > > > > also add scale.model=TRUE
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > for 'besag' and 'rw1' which are intrinsice, then constr=TRUE is
> > > > > > > > > default.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > you add more constraints with the argument 'extraconstr' if needed.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > On Fri, 2024-03-01 at 22:02 -0800, Reza Hajipour wrote:
> > > > > > > > > > Hello
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > I want to add a sum-to-zero constraint on the random effects of a
> > > > > > > > > > spatio-temporal model. Is it enough to put  constr=TRUE   as
> > > > > > > > > > follows:
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > formula <- O ~ X +
> > > > > > > > > >   f(ID.area, model="besag", graph=.... , constr=TRUE, rankdef=1) +
> > > > > > > > > >   f(ID.year, model="rw1", constr=TRUE, rankdef=1)

messages.subject: Fast computation in INLA
messages.body_plain:
Hi INLA members,

I am trying to compute a poisson model with several random effects (10) and a set of fixed effects. It is taking very long time to run in HPC. Is there any suggestions by controlling a few control.inla parameters for fast computation in INLA?

I do have a large data  with 2,435,419 rows. Any suggestions will help.

Alokesh.

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Fast computation in INLA
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Because the computation time is linear in the number of data entries, what matters for computation speed in INLA is the distribution/size of the random effects (sometimes if it is correctly specified from the computation point of view) and the number of hyper-parameters. The total computation time the setup time plus the time per iteration times the number of function evaluations. Can you say something about it?

best regards,
Elias

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Random effect in posterior predictive distribution
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Random effect in posterior predictive distribution
messages.body_plain:
If you want to work with samples of hyperparameters, it is better to use inla.hyperpar.sample() instead.

The inla.posterior.sample() sample hyperparameters accounting for the int.strategy you have set to fit the model. Given these samples, then sample the latent variables. Therefore, with int.strategy = "ccd" or int.strategy = "grid" you will have samples with hyperparameters "integrated out". The result of this function is a list and the i-th element of such list contains the sample for the hyperparamters (h_i) and the latent variables sampled give h_i.

best regards,
Elias

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] sum-to-zero constraint
messages.body_plain:
Thank you.

When fitting Knorr-Held models, using "rw1" and "besag" in the group did not take into account the required constraints. Is it the same for using "ar1" in the group?

Elias T. Krainski <eliask...@gmail.com> 于2024年5月12日周日 14:33写道：

> The 'iid' models do not need constr = TRUE.
>
>
> On Sat, 11 May 2024 at 19:15, FU peter <fupe...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Hello
> >
> > When using ar1 as a time effect, do the following models need to add additional constraints?
> > Do ID.year and ID.year1 need to add constr=TRUE?
> >
> > st2<- O ~ 1+f(ID.city,model="bym",graph=g,scale.model = T,constr=T,hyper=pc1)+
> >   f(ID.year,model="ar1",hyper=pc2,constr=T)+
> >   f(ID.year1, model = "iid",hyper=pc2,constr=T)+
> >   f(ID.city1,model="iid",hyper=pc2,group=ID.year2,control.group = list(model="ar1"))
> >
> > Elias T. Krainski <eliask...@gmail.com> 于2024年3月7日周四 19:30写道：
> > > This fits (beta + beta_i + beta_t) X_it (although the indexing here is not very precise) and having constraints in both 'rw2' and 'besag' is fine. But this is not yet a spatio-temporal model for the regression coefficient, where you would have beta_it.
> > >
> > > On Thu, 7 Mar 2024 at 13:15, Reza Hajipour <rehaj...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > It's great. Thank you.
> > > >
> > > > Yes, I have both fixed slop and random slop covariates. In this case, as you mentioned, 'beta' and 'beta_i' interact, so we need the constraint.
> > > >
> > > > I am fitting a spatio-temporal model with varying coefficients (random slop) covariates. If we have evidence that covariates vary across regions over time, is the model as follows?
> > > >
> > > > formula <- O ~ X +
> > > > f(ID.area1, X, model="besag", graph=TR.adj, constr=T) +
> > > > f(ID.year1, X, model="rw2", constr=T) +
> > > > f(ID.area2, model="besag", graph=TR.adj, constr=T) +
> > > > f(ID.area3, model="iid", constr=F) +
> > > > f(ID.year2, model="rw2", constr=T) +
> > > > f(ID.year3, model="iid", constr=F)
> > > >
> > > > Is (beta + beta_i) X_it enough or we need (beta + beta_i + beta_t) X_it? I mean is f(ID.year1, X, model="rw2", constr=T) necessary or not?
> > > >
> > > > On Thursday 7 March 2024 at 11:38:12 UTC+3:30 Elias T. Krainski wrote:
> > > > >  For this case, you have to consider either having "+ X" or not. If you have it, the constraint is needed, otherwise not. This will lead to having either (beta + beta_i) X_i (where beta_i should be constrained) or just beta_i X_i.
> > > > >
> > > > > On Thu, 7 Mar 2024 at 10:23, Reza Hajipour <rehaj...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > Thank you so much. It was so helpful for me.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > As you explained and based on the articles I have studied, the models with improper joint distribution like ICAR, leading to an identifiability problem with the model intercept.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > My model also includes the spatial varying coefficient covariates (along with fixed effect intercept) as follow:
> > > > > >
> > > > > > formula <- O ~ X +   f(ID.area1, X, model="besag", graph=TR.adj, constr=T) +
> > > > > >   f(ID.area2, model="besag", graph=TR.adj, constr=T) +
> > > > > >   f(ID.area3, model="iid", constr=F)
> > > > > >
> > > > > > In this case, does the ICAR specification of covariate 'X' again lead to an identifiability problem with the model intercept (does it interact with the model intercept) and is the constraint necessary or not?
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > On Thursday 7 March 2024 at 09:59:30 UTC+3:30 Elias T. Krainski wrote:
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Hi,
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > You do not always need constr = TRUE. It is not needed for 'iid' model, or any other model with proper joint distribution. But sometimes you want it, for example for the case of having a long range correlation that interacts with some other model component. You only need constraint in intrinsic models if another model component includes its null space.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Please take a look at the example below, where I illustrate the fact that you do not always need to add a constraint while working with intrinsic models.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > library(INLA)
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > n <- 30
> > > > > > > x <- scale(cumsum(rnorm(n)))
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > plot(x)
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > y <- rpois(n, exp(2 + x))
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > fit1 <- inla(
> > > > > > >     y ~ f(i, model = 'rw1'),
> > > > > > >     data = list(i = 1:n, y = y),
> > > > > > >     family = 'poisson'
> > > > > > > )
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > ## The intercept captures the overall mean
> > > > > > > fit1$summary.fix
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > ## posterior mean for the constrained random effect is around zero
> > > > > > > summary(fit1$summary.random$i$mean)
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > ## Now, take the intercept ou of the linear predictor
> > > > > > > ## Then, the constraint in the random effect is no longer needed
> > > > > > > fit2 <- inla(
> > > > > > >     y ~ 0 + f(i, model = 'rw1', constr = FALSE),
> > > > > > >     data = list(i = 1:n, y = y),
> > > > > > >     family = 'poisson'
> > > > > > > )
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > ## unconstrained random effect is around the intercept (not fitted separately)
> > > > > > > summary(fit2$summary.random$i$mean)
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > ## However, the fitted values are similar (not exactly the same as the priors are different and there are some small numerical differences while doing the computations)
> > > > > > > summary(fit1$summary.fitted.values$mean)
> > > > > > > summary(fit2$summary.fitted.values$mean)
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > regards,
> > > > > > > Elias
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > On Thu, 7 Mar 2024 at 08:34, Reza Hajipour <rehaj...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > > > sum-to-zero constraints ensure the identifiability, if yes, is it necessary to have this constraint on 'iid' parts, as follows?
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > formula <- O ~ X +
> > > > > > > >   f(ID.area, model="besag", graph=.... , constr=TRUE) +
> > > > > > > >   f(ID.area1, model="iid", constr=TRUE) +
> > > > > > > >   f(ID.year, model="rw2", constr=TRUE) +
> > > > > > > >   f(ID.year1, model="iid", constr=TRUE)
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > As you mentioned the constr=TRUE is default, if I don't add it to f(...) parts of the above formula, the conster is True and the sum-to-zero constraint is done for all random effects?
> > > > > > > > On Saturday 2 March 2024 at 19:04:36 UTC+3:30 Helpdesk (Haavard Rue) wrote:
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > in this case the constr=T will only impose a constraint on the 'besag'
> > > > > > > > > part of the model, not the 'iid'
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > On Sat, 2024-03-02 at 07:13 -0800, Reza Hajipour wrote:
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > Thank you.
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > What about the "BYM" model where we have two random effects, one with
> > > > > > > > > > ICAR prior and one with gaussian prior, does it give sum-to-zero as

messages.subject: Doubt about lognormal model in INLA
messages.subject_clean: Doubt about lognormal model in INLA
messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA community

I am working in a problem where I am interested in having only positive values in the support of the answer variable. I was initially working with the Guassian model trying to control the support with the use of prior but those prior ended being too informative which is something I do not want in this case. So the next option was to use a lognormal model but it is not clear for me if INLA takes the log of only the answer, only of the covariables or both. I mean this

Option 1:

log(y)~Beta_0+x1+x2

Option 2:

y ~ Beta_0 + log(x1) + log(x2)

Option 3:

log(y)~Beta_0+log(x1)+log(x2)

I am interested to return the log transformation to have the data in the original scale having also the benefit of all being positive, and the best case would be option 1, that would be

exp(model$summary$fitted.values)

Right? Or does INLA make any other process with the lognormal model that needs to be known to have the data in the original scale or to work with the lognormal model in general?

Thank you

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] sum-to-zero constraint
messages.body_plain:
Yes.

On Sun, 12 May 2024, 11:07 FU peter, <fupe...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Thank you.
>
> When fitting Knorr-Held models, using "rw1" and "besag" in the group did not take into account the required constraints. Is it the same for using "ar1" in the group?
>
> Elias T. Krainski <eliask...@gmail.com> 于2024年5月12日周日 14:33写道：
> > The 'iid' models do not need constr = TRUE.
> >
> >
> > On Sat, 11 May 2024 at 19:15, FU peter <fupe...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > Hello
> > >
> > > When using ar1 as a time effect, do the following models need to add additional constraints?
> > > Do ID.year and ID.year1 need to add constr=TRUE?
> > >
> > > st2<- O ~ 1+f(ID.city,model="bym",graph=g,scale.model = T,constr=T,hyper=pc1)+
> > >   f(ID.year,model="ar1",hyper=pc2,constr=T)+
> > >   f(ID.year1, model = "iid",hyper=pc2,constr=T)+
> > >   f(ID.city1,model="iid",hyper=pc2,group=ID.year2,control.group = list(model="ar1"))
> > >
> > > Elias T. Krainski <eliask...@gmail.com> 于2024年3月7日周四 19:30写道：
> > > > This fits (beta + beta_i + beta_t) X_it (although the indexing here is not very precise) and having constraints in both 'rw2' and 'besag' is fine. But this is not yet a spatio-temporal model for the regression coefficient, where you would have beta_it.
> > > >
> > > > On Thu, 7 Mar 2024 at 13:15, Reza Hajipour <rehaj...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > It's great. Thank you.
> > > > >
> > > > > Yes, I have both fixed slop and random slop covariates. In this case, as you mentioned, 'beta' and 'beta_i' interact, so we need the constraint.
> > > > >
> > > > > I am fitting a spatio-temporal model with varying coefficients (random slop) covariates. If we have evidence that covariates vary across regions over time, is the model as follows?
> > > > >
> > > > > formula <- O ~ X +
> > > > > f(ID.area1, X, model="besag", graph=TR.adj, constr=T) +
> > > > > f(ID.year1, X, model="rw2", constr=T) +
> > > > > f(ID.area2, model="besag", graph=TR.adj, constr=T) +
> > > > > f(ID.area3, model="iid", constr=F) +
> > > > > f(ID.year2, model="rw2", constr=T) +
> > > > > f(ID.year3, model="iid", constr=F)
> > > > >
> > > > > Is (beta + beta_i) X_it enough or we need (beta + beta_i + beta_t) X_it? I mean is f(ID.year1, X, model="rw2", constr=T) necessary or not?
> > > > >
> > > > > On Thursday 7 March 2024 at 11:38:12 UTC+3:30 Elias T. Krainski wrote:
> > > > > >  For this case, you have to consider either having "+ X" or not. If you have it, the constraint is needed, otherwise not. This will lead to having either (beta + beta_i) X_i (where beta_i should be constrained) or just beta_i X_i.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > On Thu, 7 Mar 2024 at 10:23, Reza Hajipour <rehaj...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > > Thank you so much. It was so helpful for me.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > As you explained and based on the articles I have studied, the models with improper joint distribution like ICAR, leading to an identifiability problem with the model intercept.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > My model also includes the spatial varying coefficient covariates (along with fixed effect intercept) as follow:
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > formula <- O ~ X +   f(ID.area1, X, model="besag", graph=TR.adj, constr=T) +
> > > > > > >   f(ID.area2, model="besag", graph=TR.adj, constr=T) +
> > > > > > >   f(ID.area3, model="iid", constr=F)
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > In this case, does the ICAR specification of covariate 'X' again lead to an identifiability problem with the model intercept (does it interact with the model intercept) and is the constraint necessary or not?
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > On Thursday 7 March 2024 at 09:59:30 UTC+3:30 Elias T. Krainski wrote:
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > Hi,
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > You do not always need constr = TRUE. It is not needed for 'iid' model, or any other model with proper joint distribution. But sometimes you want it, for example for the case of having a long range correlation that interacts with some other model component. You only need constraint in intrinsic models if another model component includes its null space.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > Please take a look at the example below, where I illustrate the fact that you do not always need to add a constraint while working with intrinsic models.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > library(INLA)
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > n <- 30
> > > > > > > > x <- scale(cumsum(rnorm(n)))
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > plot(x)
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > y <- rpois(n, exp(2 + x))
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > fit1 <- inla(
> > > > > > > >     y ~ f(i, model = 'rw1'),
> > > > > > > >     data = list(i = 1:n, y = y),
> > > > > > > >     family = 'poisson'
> > > > > > > > )
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > ## The intercept captures the overall mean
> > > > > > > > fit1$summary.fix
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > ## posterior mean for the constrained random effect is around zero
> > > > > > > > summary(fit1$summary.random$i$mean)
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > ## Now, take the intercept ou of the linear predictor
> > > > > > > > ## Then, the constraint in the random effect is no longer needed
> > > > > > > > fit2 <- inla(
> > > > > > > >     y ~ 0 + f(i, model = 'rw1', constr = FALSE),
> > > > > > > >     data = list(i = 1:n, y = y),
> > > > > > > >     family = 'poisson'
> > > > > > > > )
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > ## unconstrained random effect is around the intercept (not fitted separately)
> > > > > > > > summary(fit2$summary.random$i$mean)
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > ## However, the fitted values are similar (not exactly the same as the priors are different and there are some small numerical differences while doing the computations)
> > > > > > > > summary(fit1$summary.fitted.values$mean)
> > > > > > > > summary(fit2$summary.fitted.values$mean)
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > regards,
> > > > > > > > Elias
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > On Thu, 7 Mar 2024 at 08:34, Reza Hajipour <rehaj...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > > > > sum-to-zero constraints ensure the identifiability, if yes, is it necessary to have this constraint on 'iid' parts, as follows?
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > formula <- O ~ X +
> > > > > > > > >   f(ID.area, model="besag", graph=.... , constr=TRUE) +
> > > > > > > > >   f(ID.area1, model="iid", constr=TRUE) +
> > > > > > > > >   f(ID.year, model="rw2", constr=TRUE) +
> > > > > > > > >   f(ID.year1, model="iid", constr=TRUE)
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > As you mentioned the constr=TRUE is default, if I don't add it to f(...) parts of the above formula, the conster is True and the sum-to-zero constraint is done for all random effects?
> > > > > > > > > On Saturday 2 March 2024 at 19:04:36 UTC+3:30 Helpdesk (Haavard Rue) wrote:
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > in this case the constr=T will only impose a constraint on the 'besag'
> > > > > > > > > > part of the model, not the 'iid'
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > On Sat, 2024-03-02 at 07:13 -0800, Reza Hajipour wrote:
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > Thank you.
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > What about the "BYM" model where we have two random effects, one with
> > > > > > > > > > > ICAR prior and one with gaussian prior, does it give sum-to-zero as
> > > > > > > > > > > follows:
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > f(ID.area, model="BYM", graph=.... , constr=TRUE, rankdef=1)
> > > > > > > > > > > On Saturday 2 March 2024 at 13:04:09 UTC+3:30 Helpdesk (Haavard Rue)
> > > > > > > > > > > wrote:
> > > > > > > > > > > > yes, this gives a sum-to-zero constraint. for the besag and rw1 I
> > > > > > > > > > > > would

messages.subject: inlabru fit the same LGCP on multiple datasets
messages.subject_clean: inlabru fit the same LGCP on multiple datasets
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am trying to fit a LGCP model for which I have a Matern field and a spatial covariate in inlabru, this is how I construct the model and run the  inference for a single data set

spde <- inla.spde2.pcmatern(mesh = mesh, prior.range = c(1, 0.01),  prior.sigma = c(3.0, 0.01))

model <- coordinates ~ DM(f.DM(.data.), model = "linear") +  f(coordinates, model = spde) +     Intercept(1)

fit <- inlabru::lgcp(components=model, data=spdf.pp, samplers = sampler.spdf , domain = list(coordinates = mesh))

However, I have multiple datasets (set of points and covariate map and a different study region) and I want to fit them to the model assuming they are generated from the same process. Therefore, I want a posterior distribution for the range, sigma, the coefficient of the covariate and the intercept using all the data.

 I believe this has to to do with the Multiple likelihoods, LGCPs - Multiple Likelihoods • inlabru (inlabru-org.github.io) <https://inlabru-org.github.io/inlabru/articles/2d_lgcp_multilikelihood.html>, however I am really lost in implementing as in my case I have different mesh, and a different covariate map for each data set.

Could you help me out on how I could translate the above piece of code into one that takes into account multiple datasets ( set of points, covariates, regions/mesh)?

Thank you in advance, best regards,
Kyriacos Nicolaou

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] inlabru fit the same LGCP on multiple datasets
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] inlabru fit the same LGCP on multiple datasets
messages.body_plain:
﻿Hi,
This is an interesting case.

For the SPDE, one option is if you can make a joint mesh instead of having them as separate meshes. They don’t need to be geographically connected. As long as they are part of the same mesh object and the regions don’t overlap, you’ll get the effect you describe, where it’s the same SPDE model for all the regions.

For the covariate, your can let your f.DM() function take an additional argument with a vector that says which “covariate map” to apply. Or an argument with a scalar that says what to do, and use the _eval feature in the predictor, like this:
Form1 <- DM_eval(f.DM(.data., 1)) + f
Form2 <- DM_eval(f.DM(.data., 2)) + f
etc.
With that option, you can use different f.DM functions for each dataset as well. The component definition can be simply DM(1).

Finn

messages.subject: Binomial-Poisson joint model: covariance matrix of the fixed effects
messages.subject_clean: Binomial-Poisson joint model: covariance matrix of the fixed effects
messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA community

I have a spatiotemporal joint Binomial-Poisson model with this definition:

r_ijk  ~ Binomial (n_ijk, p_ijk )
logit⁡(p_ijk)= β_01 + β_1k1 + β_21[immune]_ijk + γ_k1*[immune]_ijk +  ν_(i1) + γ_(j1) + δ(ij1)

O_ij  ~ Poisson (N_ij,IR_ij )
log⁡(IR_ij)= β_02+  β_1k2   + β_22 [immune]_ijk   + γ_k2*[immune]_ijk + ν_(i2) + γ_(j2) + δ(ij1)

with  i = areal unit (1,...,93), j = temporal unit (1,...,16), k = age groups (1,...,8), ν_(i1) & ν_(i2) spatial structured random effect, γ_(j1) & γ_(j2) temporal structured random effect, δ_(ij1) & δ_(ij2) spatiotemporal interaction. The data are structured for a joint model fit (in a list with Y as a matrix) with the following model formula:

mod <- Y ~ -1 + intercept + age.bin * immune.bin + age.pois * immune.pois + f(idarea.all.1, model = "bym2", graph = gDIST, group = g.nu <http://g.nu>, scale.model = TRUE) + f(idperiod.all.1, model = "rw1", group = g.gamma) + f(idareaperiod.all.1, model = "iid", group = g.delta)

My questions are:
Is it possible to get the covariance matrix of the linear fixed effects?
If I remove all f() statements, will INLA automatically fit a joint model with only fixed effects? If this is not the case, would it be possible to fit such model in INLA?
Thank you.

Kind regards,
Yessika

and then model using

lgcp(formula, data, ips)

messages.body_plain:
n = 10^4
x = rnorm(n,  sd = 0.2)
eta = 3 + x
E = runif(n, min = 1, max=10)
E[] =1

size = 20
q = E*exp(eta);
quantile <- 0.5
p = 1.0 - qbeta(quantile, q + 1.0, size, lower.tail = FALSE);
lambda = size * (1.0 - p) / p / E;
mu = E * lambda
y = rnbinom(n, size, mu=mu)

r = inla(y ~ 1 + x, data = data.frame(y, x, E),
         family = "nbinomial", E=E, verbose=T)

summary(r)

> > > > > > variable with 0 somewhere in the middle of the range is less likely to

messages.body_plain:
Dear Charlotte,

Try adding the polynomial  to the dataframe and then add them to the stack. The example below does this only for the sand dynamics.

X70 = data.frame(Intercept = rep(1, N70),

                 sanddynamics_1 = poly(strandline70$dyn_mean, 2)[, 1],
                 sanddynamics_2 = poly(strandline70$dyn_mean), 2[, 2],
                 springtide = strandline70$spr_mean,

)
StackFit = inla.stack(tag = "Fit",
                          data = list(y = strandline70$Abundance_median),
                          A = list(A3, 1),
                          effects = list(w3.index, X70))

f0 = y ~ -1 + Intercept + sanddynamics_1 + sanddynamics_2

Best regards,

> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > I would recommend using poly(A, 2) instead of A + I(A^2). poly()
> > > > > > > generates orthogonal variables whereas A + I(A^2) might lead to highly
> > > > > > > correlated variables.
> > > > > > > Another option is to center A to a sensible point within its range and
> > > > > > > scale it by multiplying it by some power of 10. The result should be a
> > > > > > > variable with a range that somewhat resembles c(-1, 1). Squaring a
> > > > > > > variable with 0 somewhere in the middle of the range is less likely to
> > > > > > > be highly correlated than squaring a variable with 0 outside of the
> > > > > > > range of the data. Scaling ensures that the squared covariates don't
> > > > > > > get very large or very small.

> > > > > > > You might want to try it on a small dataset before running it on the

messages.subject: inference on a LGCP with two latent random fields?
messages.subject_clean: inference on a LGCP with two latent random fields?
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I have point patterns whose heterogeneity seems to be in two length scales, one larger than the other. The big length scale is on the order of the domain size, and the smaller one appears (at least to me) as smaller "clusters" in this bigger cloud of points
,

Therefore I was considering to fit a LGCP with two latent random fields, one with a prior biasing large rho, comparable to the size of the domain, and a random field with a prior for much smaller rho to capture the little clusters. the model is this:

maternl <- inla.spde2.pcmatern(mesh,
                                prior.sigma = c(2, 0.01),
                                prior.range = c(10, 0.01)
)

materns <- inla.spde2.pcmatern(mesh,
                              prior.sigma = c(1, 0.01),
                              prior.range = c(10, 0.99)
)

model <- coordinates ~
  fieldl(coordinates,model = maternl) +
  fields(coordinates,model = materns) +
  Intercept(1)

 The code seems to run in inlabru and give reasonable results, but I am wondering if it is tractable problem by inla and inlabru in particular and not just a non-sense result ?

Thank you,
Kyriacos Nicolaou

>
> For the covariate, your can let your f.DM() function take an additional argument with a vector that says which “covariate map” to apply. Or an argument with a scalar that says what to do, and use the _eval feature in the predictor, like this:
> Form1 <- DM_eval(f.DM(.data., 1)) + f
> Form2 <- DM_eval(f.DM(.data., 2)) + f
> etc.
> With that option, you can use different f.DM functions for each dataset as well. The component definition can be simply DM(1).

Yes, the principle of having two fields with different spatial “range responsibility” you describe is sound.
There would be some “fine print” about strict identifiability, but that doesn’t matter much if it seems practically identifiable, and the main focus is the combined effect of the two fields.
Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] sum-to-zero constraint
messages.body_plain:
the recommentation is to use 'bym2' instead of 'bym', and for this, constr=T is
default.

you do not need, formally, the constr=T, for ID.year and ID.year1, but due to
confounding, sometimes this is done. especially for shorter `in time' data.
constr=T also make less informative priors 'less wrong'.

I guess you see the potential confounding for ar1 and iid for year, if the years
are few...

On Sun, 2024-05-12 at 00:14 +0800, FU peter wrote:
> Hello
>
> When using ar1 as a time effect, do the following models need to add
> additional constraints?
> Do ID.year and ID.year1 need to add constr=TRUE?
>
> st2<- O ~ 1+f(ID.city,model="bym",graph=g,scale.model = T,constr=T,hyper=pc1)+
>   f(ID.year,model="ar1",hyper=pc2,constr=T)+
>   f(ID.year1, model = "iid",hyper=pc2,constr=T)+
>   f(ID.city1,model="iid",hyper=pc2,group=ID.year2,control.group =
> list(model="ar1"))
>
> Elias T. Krainski <eliask...@gmail.com> 于2024年3月7日周四 19:30写道：
> > This fits (beta + beta_i + beta_t) X_it (although the indexing here is not
> > very precise) and having constraints in both 'rw2' and 'besag' is fine. But
> > this is not yet a spatio-temporal model for the regression coefficient,
> > where you would have beta_it.
> >
> > On Thu, 7 Mar 2024 at 13:15, Reza Hajipour <rehaj...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > It's great. Thank you.
> > >
> > > Yes, I have both fixed slop and random slop covariates. In this case, as
> > > you mentioned, 'beta' and 'beta_i' interact, so we need the constraint.
> > >
> > > I am fitting a spatio-temporal model with varying coefficients (random
> > > slop) covariates. If we have evidence that covariates vary across regions
> > > over time, is the model as follows?
> > >
> > > formula <- O ~ X +
> > > f(ID.area1, X, model="besag", graph=TR.adj, constr=T) +
> > > f(ID.year1, X, model="rw2", constr=T) +
> > > f(ID.area2, model="besag", graph=TR.adj, constr=T) +
> > > f(ID.area3, model="iid", constr=F) +
> > > f(ID.year2, model="rw2", constr=T) +
> > > f(ID.year3, model="iid", constr=F)
> > >
> > > Is (beta + beta_i) X_it enough or we need (beta + beta_i + beta_t) X_it? I
> > > mean is f(ID.year1, X, model="rw2", constr=T) necessary or not?
> > >
> > > On Thursday 7 March 2024 at 11:38:12 UTC+3:30 Elias T. Krainski wrote:
> > > >  For this case, you have to consider either having "+ X" or not. If you
> > > > have it, the constraint is needed, otherwise not. This will lead to
> > > > having either (beta + beta_i) X_i (where beta_i should be constrained)
> > > > or just beta_i X_i.
> > > >
> > > > On Thu, 7 Mar 2024 at 10:23, Reza Hajipour <rehaj...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > Thank you so much. It was so helpful for me.
> > > > >
> > > > > As you explained and based on the articles I have studied, the models
> > > > > with improper joint distribution like ICAR, leading to an
> > > > > identifiability problem with the model intercept.
> > > > >
> > > > > My model also includes the spatial varying coefficient covariates
> > > > > (along with fixed effect intercept) as follow:
> > > > >
> > > > > formula <- O ~ X +   f(ID.area1, X, model="besag", graph=TR.adj,
> > > > > constr=T) +
> > > > >   f(ID.area2, model="besag", graph=TR.adj, constr=T) +
> > > > >   f(ID.area3, model="iid", constr=F)
> > > > >
> > > > > In this case, does the ICAR specification of covariate 'X' again lead
> > > > > to an identifiability problem with the model intercept (does it
> > > > > interact with the model intercept) and is the constraint necessary or
> > > > > not?
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > On Thursday 7 March 2024 at 09:59:30 UTC+3:30 Elias T. Krainski wrote:
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Hi,
> > > > > >
> > > > > > You do not always need constr = TRUE. It is not needed for 'iid'
> > > > > > model, or any other model with proper joint distribution. But
> > > > > > sometimes you want it, for example for the case of having a long
> > > > > > range correlation that interacts with some other model component.
> > > > > > You only need constraint in intrinsic models if another model
> > > > > > component includes its null space.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Please take a look at the example below, where I illustrate the fact
> > > > > > that you do not always need to add a constraint while working with
> > > > > > intrinsic models.
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > library(INLA)
> > > > > >
> > > > > > n <- 30
> > > > > > x <- scale(cumsum(rnorm(n)))
> > > > > >
> > > > > > plot(x)
> > > > > >
> > > > > > y <- rpois(n, exp(2 + x))
> > > > > >
> > > > > > fit1 <- inla(
> > > > > >     y ~ f(i, model = 'rw1'),
> > > > > >     data = list(i = 1:n, y = y),
> > > > > >     family = 'poisson'
> > > > > > )
> > > > > >
> > > > > > ## The intercept captures the overall mean
> > > > > > fit1$summary.fix
> > > > > >
> > > > > > ## posterior mean for the constrained random effect is around zero
> > > > > > summary(fit1$summary.random$i$mean)
> > > > > >
> > > > > > ## Now, take the intercept ou of the linear predictor
> > > > > > ## Then, the constraint in the random effect is no longer needed
> > > > > > fit2 <- inla(
> > > > > >     y ~ 0 + f(i, model = 'rw1', constr = FALSE),
> > > > > >     data = list(i = 1:n, y = y),
> > > > > >     family = 'poisson'
> > > > > > )
> > > > > >
> > > > > > ## unconstrained random effect is around the intercept (not fitted
> > > > > > separately)
> > > > > > summary(fit2$summary.random$i$mean)
> > > > > >
> > > > > > ## However, the fitted values are similar (not exactly the same as
> > > > > > the priors are different and there are some small numerical
> > > > > > differences while doing the computations)
> > > > > > summary(fit1$summary.fitted.values$mean)
> > > > > > summary(fit2$summary.fitted.values$mean)
> > > > > >
> > > > > > regards,
> > > > > > Elias
> > > > > >
> > > > > > On Thu, 7 Mar 2024 at 08:34, Reza Hajipour <rehaj...@gmail.com>
> > > > > > wrote:
> > > > > > > sum-to-zero constraints ensure the identifiability, if yes, is it
> > > > > > > necessary to have this constraint on 'iid' parts, as follows?
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > formula <- O ~ X +
> > > > > > >   f(ID.area, model="besag", graph=.... , constr=TRUE) +
> > > > > > >   f(ID.area1, model="iid", constr=TRUE) +
> > > > > > >   f(ID.year, model="rw2", constr=TRUE) +
> > > > > > >   f(ID.year1, model="iid", constr=TRUE)
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > As you mentioned the constr=TRUE is default, if I don't add it to
> > > > > > > f(...) parts of the above formula, the conster is True and the
> > > > > > > sum-to-zero constraint is done for all random effects?
> > > > > > > On Saturday 2 March 2024 at 19:04:36 UTC+3:30 Helpdesk (Haavard
> > > > > > > Rue) wrote:
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > in this case the constr=T will only impose a constraint on the
> > > > > > > > 'besag'
> > > > > > > > part of the model, not the 'iid'
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > On Sat, 2024-03-02 at 07:13 -0800, Reza Hajipour wrote:
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > Thank you.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > What about the "BYM" model where we have two random effects,
> > > > > > > > > one with
> > > > > > > > > ICAR prior and one with gaussian prior, does it give sum-to-
> > > > > > > > > zero as
> > > > > > > > > follows:
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > f(ID.area, model="BYM", graph=.... , constr=TRUE, rankdef=1)
> > > > > > > > > On Saturday 2 March 2024 at 13:04:09 UTC+3:30 Helpdesk
> > > > > > > > > (Haavard Rue)
> > > > > > > > > wrote:
> > > > > > > > > > yes, this gives a sum-to-zero constraint. for the besag and
> > > > > > > > > > rw1 I
> > > > > > > > > > would
> > > > > > > > > > also add scale.model=TRUE
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > for 'besag' and 'rw1' which are intrinsice, then constr=TRUE
> > > > > > > > > > is
> > > > > > > > > > default.
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > you add more constraints with the argument 'extraconstr' if
> > > > > > > > > > needed.
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > On Fri, 2024-03-01 at 22:02 -0800, Reza Hajipour wrote:
> > > > > > > > > > > Hello

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Formula including quadratic terms
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

Thank you, it works!
The full code:

N70 = nrow(strandline70)
X70 = data.frame(Intercept = rep(1, N70),

                 sanddynamics_1 = poly(strandline70$dyn_mean, 2)[, 1],

                 sanddynamics_2 = poly(strandline70$dyn_mean, 2)[, 2],
                 springtide_1 = poly(strandline70$spr_mean, 2)[, 1],
                 springtide_2 = poly(strandline70$spr_mean, 2)[, 2])

StackFit = inla.stack(tag = "Fit",
                          data = list(y = strandline70$Abundance_median),
                          A = list(A3, 1),
                          effects = list(w3.index, X70))

FIT = inla.stack(StackFit)

#### null function
f0 = y ~ -1 + Intercept + sanddynamics_1 + sanddynamics_2 + springtide_1 + springtide_2

inla0 = inla(f0,
            family = "zeroinflatedpoisson0",
            control.compute = list(waic = TRUE),
            data = inla.stack.data(StackFit),
            control.predictor = list(A = inla.stack.A(StackFit)))

#### full function
f = y ~ -1 + Intercept + sanddynamics_1 + sanddynamics_2 + springtide_1 + springtide_2 +

  f(w, model = spde, group = w.group, control.group = list(model = "ar1"))

inla_sp = inla(f,
                family = "zeroinflatedpoisson0",
                data = inla.stack.data(StackFit),
                control.compute = list(waic=T),

                control.predictor = list(A = inla.stack.A(StackFit)))

Kind regards,
Charlotte

Hi R-INLA community,

In an attempt to plot the mean and SD of the spatial random field onto my mesh, I came across an error that I can't solve.

Loc = cbind(strandline70$X, strandline70$Y)
mesh = inla.mesh.2d(boundary = beaches,
                        loc = Loc,
                        max.edge = max_edge,
                        cutoff = 1000)

w.mean   = inla_sp$summary.random$w$mean
w.sd <http://w.sd> =  inla_sp$summary.random$w$sd
projection = inla.mesh.projector(mesh)
w.pmf  = inla.mesh.project(projection, w.mean)

w.pmf = inla.mesh.project(projection, w.mean) Error in projector$proj$A %*% as.vector(field) : non-conformable arguments

My model is spatio-temporal, so I assume it is because there exist 6 spatial fields (6 years of data). How do I plot this for every year? Apologies if this question has been answered already.

Kind regards,
Charlotte Taelman

Hi Charlotte,
yes, the quickest solution is to extract only the part of w.mean
corresponding to a single year, and give only that to the project
function, and repeat for each year.
w.mean holds the data year, by year, so
w.mean[seq_len(mesh$n)+(year_idx - 1)*mesh$n] should do the trick.
Finn

messages.body_plain:
Dear Finn, thanks!

I had found a similar answer in Chapter 15 of the book (count data warblers), so I'll add my code to this thread below:

w.pm <http://w.pm>   = inla_sp$summary.random$w$mean # posterior mean values of spatial random field
w.sd <http://w.sd> =  inla_sp$summary.random$w$sd # uncertainty on posterior mean of spatial random field
w.proj = inla.mesh.projector(mesh)
w3.index = inla.spde.make.index(name = 'w',
                             n.spde = mesh$n,
                             n.group = length(unique(df70$JAAR)))

w.pmf <- list() # six years of data
for (i in 1:length(unique(df70$JAAR))){
   w.pmf[[i]] <- inla.mesh.project(w.proj, w.pm <http://w.pm>[w3.index$w.group==i])
}

sp_df_all = data.frame()
for (y in c(1:length(unique(df70$JAAR)))){
  grid  = expand.grid(X = w.proj$x, Y = w.proj$y)
  sp_df = data.frame(x = grid[,1],
                     y = grid[,2],
                     z = as.vector(w.pmf[[y]]))
  sp_df$YEAR = rep(y + 2016, nrow(sp_df))
  sp_df_all = rbind(sp_df, sp_df_all)
}

ggplot(sp_df_all, aes(x, y, z = z)) +
  geom_raster(aes(fill = z)) +
  labs(title = "Spatial random field", fill="Spatial field", x = "X", y = "Y") +
  theme(text = element_text(size = 25, family = "helveticanow")) +
  facet_wrap(~YEAR)

messages.subject: Inla keep failing, suddenly
messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA Development Team,

Greetings!

I am a user of the INLA package and have recently encountered a couple of issues while running some Bayesian statistical models. I am reaching out for your assistance in resolving these problems.

Issue 1: Model Execution Failure

Over the past few days, I have been using the INLA package to run several models. To my confusion, models that were previously successful are now failing to execute. I have tested with the most basic models using minimal covariates (baseline models), but the issue persists. I use the same dataset, same code, and it was still successful 3 hours ago. This issue appear suddenly and I could not solve. The error message I am receiving is as follows:
*** inla.core.safe: The inla program failed, but will rerun in case better initial values may help. try=1/1 For more details using debug=T , verbose=T
> form_i y ~ 1 + offset(logpop) + f(month, model = "rw1", hyper = hyper2.rw <http://hyper2.rw>, cyclic = TRUE, scale.model = TRUE, constr = TRUE, replicate = cityx) + f(polyid, model = "bym2", graph = nbmatrix_name, replicate = yearx, scale.model = TRUE, constr = TRUE, adjust.for.con.comp = TRUE, hyper = hyper.bym2) > # save storage by cutting all unnecessary variables and only keep specified variable > dd_i <- ddf %>% +  dplyr::select( +  city, +  cityid, +  countyid, +  county, +  year, +  month, +  total_cases, +  logpop, +  polyid, +  yearx, +  cityx, +  areaidx, +  urban_log, +  transportation_log, +  out_migration_g, +  Cropland_log, +  Forest_log, +  elevation_log +  ) %>% +  dplyr::mutate(y = total_cases) %>% +  cbind(ddf[ , grep(as.vector(fx_i$fx), names(ddf)), drop=FALSE]) > # fit model > mod_i = tryCatch( +  fitINLAModel(form_i, dd_i, family="nbinomial", verbose=TRUE), +  error = function(e) return(e) + ) [1] "head(scale)" NULL [1] "head(weights)" NULL [1] "head(Ntrials)" NULL [1] "head(offset)" NULL [1] "head(E)" NULL [1] "head(strata)" NULL [1] "head(lp.scale)" NULL [1] "head(link.covariates)" NULL [1] "MPredictor 0" [1] "NPredictor 8892" [1] "NData 8892" [1] "y...fake has length 8892" n.family 1 [1] "Entries with same length:" "city" "cityid" [4] "countyid" "county" "year" [7] "month" "total_cases" "logpop" [10] "polyid" "yearx" "cityx" [13] "areaidx" "urban_log" "transportation_log" [16] "out_migration_g" "Cropland_log" "Forest_log" [19] "elevation_log" "y...fake" *** inla.core.safe: The inla program failed, but will rerun in case better initial values may help. try=1/1 [1] "MPredictor 0" [1] "NPredictor 8892" [1] "NData 8892" [1] "y...fake has length 8892" n.family 1 [1] "Entries with same length:" "city" "cityid" [4] "countyid" "county" "year" [7] "month" "total_cases" "logpop" [10] "polyid" "yearx" "cityx" [13] "areaidx" "urban_log" "transportation_log" [16] "out_migration_g" "Cropland_log" "Forest_log" [19] "elevation_log" "y...fake"

And this is the function I used to run Inla:
fitINLAModel = function(formx, data, family, config=FALSE, verbose=TRUE, return.marginals=FALSE){

  return(

    INLA::inla(

      # formula, data and model family
      formx,
      data = data,
      family = family,
      safe = TRUE,  # enable possible restarts to improve initial values and Hessian if needed
      # fixed effects calibration
      control.fixed = list(mean.intercept=0,
                           prec.intercept=1, # precision 1
                           mean=0,
                           prec=1), # weakly regularising on fixed effects (sd of 1)

      # save predicted values on response scale
      control.predictor = list(compute=FALSE,
                               link=1),

      # items to compute
      control.compute = list(cpo=TRUE,
                             waic=TRUE,
                             dic=TRUE,
                             config=config, # set config to TRUE if want to do INLA::inla.posterior.sample()
                             return.marginals=return.marginals), # do not return marginals unless specified (saves memory)

      # configure inla approx
      control.inla = control.inla(strategy = "auto"),
      # verbose?
      inla.mode = "experimental", # new version of INLA algorithm (requires R 4.1 and INLA testing version)
      verbose = verbose,
      debug=T
    )
  )

}

Issue 2: Execution Issues with Complex Models

Assuming Issue 1 can be resolved, I would also like to inquire about handling errors when running more complex models. In my previous experience, I have noticed that adding certain covariates to the model allows it to run successfully, but introducing additional covariates sometimes causes the model to fail. Are there any general strategies or best practices you could share for dealing with this kind of situation?

I am willing to provide the relevant data and code snippets, which can be sent as attachments or through any other method you prefer.

Thank you for your time and assistance. I am looking forward to your response and hope to resolve these issues promptly to continue with my research work.

Best regards

As you guessed, predict() (and generate()) doesn't handle data objects

reasons). So for now, use sf, and see the vignette examples for how to
plot the result in a raster-like way (with gg(..., geom="tile"). From
the example in the README:

# Predict Gorilla nest intensity
lambda <- predict(
  fit,
  fm_pixels(gorillas_sf$mesh, mask = gorillas_sf$boundary),
  ~ exp(mySmooth + Intercept)
)

# Plot the result
ggplot() +
  geom_fm(data = gorillas_sf$mesh) +
  gg(lambda, geom = "tile") +
  gg(gorillas$nests, color = "red", size = 0.5, alpha = 0.5) +
  ggtitle("Nest intensity per km squared") +
  xlab("") +
  ylab("")

messages.subject_clean: Filling of NAs in rasters even though the rasters are complete
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'm running into an issue that I am not sure what's going on. I have this code:

# all comes from 03 in the correct crs (5042)
tProj_km <- CRS("+proj=stere +lat_0=-90 +lon_0=0 +k=0.994 +x_0=2000000 +y_0=2000000 +datum=WGS84 +units=km +no_defs")
locs <- readRDS("final_data/locs_100occ.rds")
max_temp <- rast("scaled/max_temp_complete.tif)

bound1 <- inla.nonconvex.hull(
    locs[[1]],
    convex = 130
   )
bound2 <- inla.nonconvex.hull(
    locs[[1]],
    convex = 500
    )

mesh2 <- inla.mesh.2d(
    boundary = list(bound1, bound2),
    max.edge=c(35,300),
    offset = c(20, 100),
    cutoff = 15,
    crs = crs(max_temp))

spde <- inla.spde2.pcmatern(mesh = mesh2,
                                prior.range = c(70, 0.1),
                                prior.sigma = c(0.5, 0.1))

fm <- coordinates ~ Intercept(1) +
       maxT(max_temp, model = "linear") +
       field(coordinates, model = spde)

mod <- lgcp(fm, locs[[1],
                   domain = list(coordinates =mesh2),
                   options = list(control.compute =
                                    list(waic = TRUE,
                                         cpo = TRUE,
                                         return.marginals.predictor = TRUE),
                                  control.inla = list(strategy = "simplified.laplace", int.strategy = 'eb'),
                                  verbose = FALSE))

But every time I run the model, I get this warning, which makes the model run much slower:

Warning in input_eval.bru_input(subcomp$input, data = lh$data, env = env,  :
  Model input 'rasters$max_temp' for 'maxT' returned some NA values.
Attempting to fill in spatially by nearest available value.
To avoid this basic covariate imputation, supply complete data.

So I checked with what essentially bru_fill_missing does from my understanding, and took the values for the raster in each vertice:

vertices <- fm_vertices(mesh2)
values <- terra::extract(max_temp, vertices)
sum(is.na <http://is.na>(values))
[1] 0

And checked if the mesh is contained within the raster (I have also plotted it), which confirms that it is inside it:

fm_bbox(mesh2)
Bounding box: (-1183.108, 4095.047) x (-449.2842,4822.1893) x (0,0)
ext(max_temp)
SpatExtent : -1780.85583654458, 6724.81805966985, -1674.95620474093, 6437.3149463939 (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax)

And just confirming my raster doesn't have any NAs:
anyNA(values(rasters$max_temp))
[1] FALSE

I can't share the raster here (it's 200MB as I have also expanded it to try to avoid this error), but I have added the mesh and the location points here.

A few more things: I'm running it on a Windows computer (R 4.3.2) and my INLA version is 24.02.09. I have also tried running it on the cluster (R 4.3.1, INLA_24.05.13-1) and I get the same warning. Running it on my Macbook (R 4.3.3, INLA_24.05.01-1) does not produce the warning; however, all the intercepts and slopes are bad. And interestingly enough, when I run a more complex mesh (with a shapefile boundary), I don't get the warning.

I have run out of ideas on what may be the problem. I have made sure it's the same CRS throughout the whole script, and I have also tried expanding the rasters even more, but that also doesn't work.

Many thanks and happy to provide more info.

messages.body_plain:
Check what manual evaluation does:
First use fm_int() with the same mesh domain and samplers info to create integration points, and call eval_spatial() with the same raster input as the model component it warns about.
Also evaluate with eval_spatial() with the point pattern location object. Then you can more easily check what values are becoming NA.
One item of concern is that you don't seem to have any "samplers" info. You should really specify the modelling region polygon explicitly, as the point process only makes sense in the sampled region, which is typically smaller than the mesh.

Plotting tye mesh on top of the raster may also help; that the mesh bounding box is inside the raster bounding box doesn't mean you shouldn't get any NAs, unless the raster has complete info in the entire box, with no "masking".

Finn
