messages.body_plain:
Thank you.
I'm using this code on the official book, and the example data has 18 years of data, is this considered few?

If AR1 doesn't need additional constraints, is it appropriate to use ‘groups’ to model spatio-temporal interactions?

Helpdesk (Haavard Rue) <he...@r-inla.org> 于2024年5月15日周三 15:48写道：

>
> the recommentation is to use 'bym2' instead of 'bym', and for this, constr=T is
> default.
>
> you do not need, formally, the constr=T, for ID.year and ID.year1, but due to
> confounding, sometimes this is done. especially for shorter `in time' data.
> constr=T also make less informative priors 'less wrong'.
>
> I guess you see the potential confounding for ar1 and iid for year, if the years
> are few...
>
>
>
> On Sun, 2024-05-12 at 00:14 +0800, FU peter wrote:
> > Hello
> >
> > When using ar1 as a time effect, do the following models need to add
> > additional constraints?
> > Do ID.year and ID.year1 need to add constr=TRUE?
> >
> > st2<- O ~ 1+f(ID.city,model="bym",graph=g,scale.model = T,constr=T,hyper=pc1)+
> >   f(ID.year,model="ar1",hyper=pc2,constr=T)+
> >   f(ID.year1, model = "iid",hyper=pc2,constr=T)+
> >   f(ID.city1,model="iid",hyper=pc2,group=ID.year2,control.group =
> > list(model="ar1"))
> >
> > Elias T. Krainski <eliask...@gmail.com> 于2024年3月7日周四 19:30写道：
> > > This fits (beta + beta_i + beta_t) X_it (although the indexing here is not
> > > very precise) and having constraints in both 'rw2' and 'besag' is fine. But
> > > this is not yet a spatio-temporal model for the regression coefficient,
> > > where you would have beta_it.
> > >
> > > On Thu, 7 Mar 2024 at 13:15, Reza Hajipour <rehaj...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > It's great. Thank you.
> > > >
> > > > Yes, I have both fixed slop and random slop covariates. In this case, as
> > > > you mentioned, 'beta' and 'beta_i' interact, so we need the constraint.
> > > >
> > > > I am fitting a spatio-temporal model with varying coefficients (random
> > > > slop) covariates. If we have evidence that covariates vary across regions
> > > > over time, is the model as follows?
> > > >
> > > > formula <- O ~ X +
> > > > f(ID.area1, X, model="besag", graph=TR.adj, constr=T) +
> > > > f(ID.year1, X, model="rw2", constr=T) +
> > > > f(ID.area2, model="besag", graph=TR.adj, constr=T) +
> > > > f(ID.area3, model="iid", constr=F) +
> > > > f(ID.year2, model="rw2", constr=T) +
> > > > f(ID.year3, model="iid", constr=F)
> > > >
> > > > Is (beta + beta_i) X_it enough or we need (beta + beta_i + beta_t) X_it? I
> > > > mean is f(ID.year1, X, model="rw2", constr=T) necessary or not?
> > > >
> > > > On Thursday 7 March 2024 at 11:38:12 UTC+3:30 Elias T. Krainski wrote:
> > > > >  For this case, you have to consider either having "+ X" or not. If you
> > > > > have it, the constraint is needed, otherwise not. This will lead to
> > > > > having either (beta + beta_i) X_i (where beta_i should be constrained)
> > > > > or just beta_i X_i.
> > > > >
> > > > > On Thu, 7 Mar 2024 at 10:23, Reza Hajipour <rehaj...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > Thank you so much. It was so helpful for me.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > As you explained and based on the articles I have studied, the models
> > > > > > with improper joint distribution like ICAR, leading to an
> > > > > > identifiability problem with the model intercept.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > My model also includes the spatial varying coefficient covariates
> > > > > > (along with fixed effect intercept) as follow:
> > > > > >
> > > > > > formula <- O ~ X +   f(ID.area1, X, model="besag", graph=TR.adj,
> > > > > > constr=T) +
> > > > > >   f(ID.area2, model="besag", graph=TR.adj, constr=T) +
> > > > > >   f(ID.area3, model="iid", constr=F)
> > > > > >
> > > > > > In this case, does the ICAR specification of covariate 'X' again lead
> > > > > > to an identifiability problem with the model intercept (does it
> > > > > > interact with the model intercept) and is the constraint necessary or
> > > > > > not?
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > On Thursday 7 March 2024 at 09:59:30 UTC+3:30 Elias T. Krainski wrote:
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Hi,
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > You do not always need constr = TRUE. It is not needed for 'iid'
> > > > > > > model, or any other model with proper joint distribution. But
> > > > > > > sometimes you want it, for example for the case of having a long
> > > > > > > range correlation that interacts with some other model component.
> > > > > > > You only need constraint in intrinsic models if another model
> > > > > > > component includes its null space.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Please take a look at the example below, where I illustrate the fact
> > > > > > > that you do not always need to add a constraint while working with
> > > > > > > intrinsic models.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > library(INLA)
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > n <- 30
> > > > > > > x <- scale(cumsum(rnorm(n)))
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > plot(x)
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > y <- rpois(n, exp(2 + x))
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > fit1 <- inla(
> > > > > > >     y ~ f(i, model = 'rw1'),
> > > > > > >     data = list(i = 1:n, y = y),
> > > > > > >     family = 'poisson'
> > > > > > > )
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > ## The intercept captures the overall mean
> > > > > > > fit1$summary.fix
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > ## posterior mean for the constrained random effect is around zero
> > > > > > > summary(fit1$summary.random$i$mean)
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > ## Now, take the intercept ou of the linear predictor
> > > > > > > ## Then, the constraint in the random effect is no longer needed
> > > > > > > fit2 <- inla(
> > > > > > >     y ~ 0 + f(i, model = 'rw1', constr = FALSE),
> > > > > > >     data = list(i = 1:n, y = y),
> > > > > > >     family = 'poisson'
> > > > > > > )
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > ## unconstrained random effect is around the intercept (not fitted
> > > > > > > separately)
> > > > > > > summary(fit2$summary.random$i$mean)
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > ## However, the fitted values are similar (not exactly the same as
> > > > > > > the priors are different and there are some small numerical
> > > > > > > differences while doing the computations)
> > > > > > > summary(fit1$summary.fitted.values$mean)
> > > > > > > summary(fit2$summary.fitted.values$mean)
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > regards,
> > > > > > > Elias
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > On Thu, 7 Mar 2024 at 08:34, Reza Hajipour <rehaj...@gmail.com>
> > > > > > > wrote:
> > > > > > > > sum-to-zero constraints ensure the identifiability, if yes, is it
> > > > > > > > necessary to have this constraint on 'iid' parts, as follows?
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > formula <- O ~ X +
> > > > > > > >   f(ID.area, model="besag", graph=.... , constr=TRUE) +
> > > > > > > >   f(ID.area1, model="iid", constr=TRUE) +
> > > > > > > >   f(ID.year, model="rw2", constr=TRUE) +
> > > > > > > >   f(ID.year1, model="iid", constr=TRUE)
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > As you mentioned the constr=TRUE is default, if I don't add it to
> > > > > > > > f(...) parts of the above formula, the conster is True and the
> > > > > > > > sum-to-zero constraint is done for all random effects?
> > > > > > > > On Saturday 2 March 2024 at 19:04:36 UTC+3:30 Helpdesk (Haavard
> > > > > > > > Rue) wrote:
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > in this case the constr=T will only impose a constraint on the
> > > > > > > > > 'besag'
> > > > > > > > > part of the model, not the 'iid'
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > On Sat, 2024-03-02 at 07:13 -0800, Reza Hajipour wrote:
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > Thank you.
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > What about the "BYM" model where we have two random effects,
> > > > > > > > > > one with
> > > > > > > > > > ICAR prior and one with gaussian prior, does it give sum-to-
> > > > > > > > > > zero as
> > > > > > > > > > follows:
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > f(ID.area, model="BYM", graph=.... , constr=TRUE, rankdef=1)
> > > > > > > > > > On Saturday 2 March 2024 at 13:04:09 UTC+3:30 Helpdesk
> > > > > > > > > > (Haavard Rue)
> > > > > > > > > > wrote:
> > > > > > > > > > > yes, this gives a sum-to-zero constraint. for the besag and
> > > > > > > > > > > rw1 I
> > > > > > > > > > > would
> > > > > > > > > > > also add scale.model=TRUE
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > for 'besag' and 'rw1' which are intrinsice, then constr=TRUE
> > > > > > > > > > > is
> > > > > > > > > > > default.
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > you add more constraints with the argument 'extraconstr' if
> > > > > > > > > > > needed.
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > On Fri, 2024-03-01 at 22:02 -0800, Reza Hajipour wrote:
> > > > > > > > > > > > Hello

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] sum-to-zero constraint
messages.body_plain:
for stability, I would add constr=T as it separate effects and avoid confounding

On Fri, 2024-05-17 at 20:22 +0800, FU peter wrote:
> Thank you.
> I'm using this code on the official book, and the example data has 18 years of
> data, is this considered few?
>
> If AR1 doesn't need additional constraints, is it appropriate to use ‘groups’
> to model spatio-temporal interactions?
>
> Helpdesk (Haavard Rue) <he...@r-inla.org> 于2024年5月15日周三 15:48写道：
> >
> > the recommentation is to use 'bym2' instead of 'bym', and for this, constr=T
> > is
> > default.
> >
> > you do not need, formally, the constr=T, for ID.year and ID.year1, but due
> > to
> > confounding, sometimes this is done. especially for shorter `in time' data.
> > constr=T also make less informative priors 'less wrong'.
> >
> > I guess you see the potential confounding for ar1 and iid for year, if the
> > years
> > are few...
> >
> >
> >
> > On Sun, 2024-05-12 at 00:14 +0800, FU peter wrote:
> > > Hello
> > >
> > > When using ar1 as a time effect, do the following models need to add
> > > additional constraints?
> > > Do ID.year and ID.year1 need to add constr=TRUE?
> > >
> > > st2<- O ~ 1+f(ID.city,model="bym",graph=g,scale.model =
> > > T,constr=T,hyper=pc1)+
> > >   f(ID.year,model="ar1",hyper=pc2,constr=T)+
> > >   f(ID.year1, model = "iid",hyper=pc2,constr=T)+
> > >   f(ID.city1,model="iid",hyper=pc2,group=ID.year2,control.group =
> > > list(model="ar1"))
> > >
> > > Elias T. Krainski <eliask...@gmail.com> 于2024年3月7日周四 19:30写道：
> > > > This fits (beta + beta_i + beta_t) X_it (although the indexing here is
> > > > not
> > > > very precise) and having constraints in both 'rw2' and 'besag' is fine.
> > > > But
> > > > this is not yet a spatio-temporal model for the regression coefficient,
> > > > where you would have beta_it.
> > > >
> > > > On Thu, 7 Mar 2024 at 13:15, Reza Hajipour <rehaj...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > It's great. Thank you.
> > > > >
> > > > > Yes, I have both fixed slop and random slop covariates. In this case,
> > > > > as
> > > > > you mentioned, 'beta' and 'beta_i' interact, so we need the
> > > > > constraint.
> > > > >
> > > > > I am fitting a spatio-temporal model with varying coefficients (random
> > > > > slop) covariates. If we have evidence that covariates vary across
> > > > > regions
> > > > > over time, is the model as follows?
> > > > >
> > > > > formula <- O ~ X +
> > > > > f(ID.area1, X, model="besag", graph=TR.adj, constr=T) +
> > > > > f(ID.year1, X, model="rw2", constr=T) +
> > > > > f(ID.area2, model="besag", graph=TR.adj, constr=T) +
> > > > > f(ID.area3, model="iid", constr=F) +
> > > > > f(ID.year2, model="rw2", constr=T) +
> > > > > f(ID.year3, model="iid", constr=F)
> > > > >
> > > > > Is (beta + beta_i) X_it enough or we need (beta + beta_i + beta_t)
> > > > > X_it? I
> > > > > mean is f(ID.year1, X, model="rw2", constr=T) necessary or not?
> > > > >
> > > > > On Thursday 7 March 2024 at 11:38:12 UTC+3:30 Elias T. Krainski wrote:
> > > > > >  For this case, you have to consider either having "+ X" or not. If
> > > > > > you
> > > > > > have it, the constraint is needed, otherwise not. This will lead to
> > > > > > having either (beta + beta_i) X_i (where beta_i should be
> > > > > > constrained)
> > > > > > or just beta_i X_i.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > On Thu, 7 Mar 2024 at 10:23, Reza Hajipour <rehaj...@gmail.com>
> > > > > > wrote:
> > > > > > > Thank you so much. It was so helpful for me.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > As you explained and based on the articles I have studied, the
> > > > > > > models
> > > > > > > with improper joint distribution like ICAR, leading to an
> > > > > > > identifiability problem with the model intercept.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > My model also includes the spatial varying coefficient covariates
> > > > > > > (along with fixed effect intercept) as follow:
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > formula <- O ~ X +   f(ID.area1, X, model="besag", graph=TR.adj,
> > > > > > > constr=T) +
> > > > > > >   f(ID.area2, model="besag", graph=TR.adj, constr=T) +
> > > > > > >   f(ID.area3, model="iid", constr=F)
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > In this case, does the ICAR specification of covariate 'X'
> > > > > > > again lead
> > > > > > > to an identifiability problem with the model intercept (does it
> > > > > > > interact with the model intercept) and is the constraint necessary
> > > > > > > or
> > > > > > > not?
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > On Thursday 7 March 2024 at 09:59:30 UTC+3:30 Elias T. Krainski
> > > > > > > wrote:
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > Hi,
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > You do not always need constr = TRUE. It is not needed for 'iid'
> > > > > > > > model, or any other model with proper joint distribution. But
> > > > > > > > sometimes you want it, for example for the case of having a long
> > > > > > > > range correlation that interacts with some other model
> > > > > > > > component.
> > > > > > > > You only need constraint in intrinsic models if another model
> > > > > > > > component includes its null space.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > Please take a look at the example below, where I illustrate the
> > > > > > > > fact
> > > > > > > > that you do not always need to add a constraint while working
> > > > > > > > with
> > > > > > > > intrinsic models.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > library(INLA)
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > n <- 30
> > > > > > > > x <- scale(cumsum(rnorm(n)))
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > plot(x)
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > y <- rpois(n, exp(2 + x))
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > fit1 <- inla(
> > > > > > > >     y ~ f(i, model = 'rw1'),
> > > > > > > >     data = list(i = 1:n, y = y),
> > > > > > > >     family = 'poisson'
> > > > > > > > )
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > ## The intercept captures the overall mean
> > > > > > > > fit1$summary.fix
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > ## posterior mean for the constrained random effect is around
> > > > > > > > zero
> > > > > > > > summary(fit1$summary.random$i$mean)
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > ## Now, take the intercept ou of the linear predictor
> > > > > > > > ## Then, the constraint in the random effect is no longer needed
> > > > > > > > fit2 <- inla(
> > > > > > > >     y ~ 0 + f(i, model = 'rw1', constr = FALSE),
> > > > > > > >     data = list(i = 1:n, y = y),
> > > > > > > >     family = 'poisson'
> > > > > > > > )
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > ## unconstrained random effect is around the intercept (not
> > > > > > > > fitted
> > > > > > > > separately)
> > > > > > > > summary(fit2$summary.random$i$mean)
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > ## However, the fitted values are similar (not exactly the same
> > > > > > > > as
> > > > > > > > the priors are different and there are some small numerical
> > > > > > > > differences while doing the computations)
> > > > > > > > summary(fit1$summary.fitted.values$mean)
> > > > > > > > summary(fit2$summary.fitted.values$mean)
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > regards,
> > > > > > > > Elias
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > On Thu, 7 Mar 2024 at 08:34, Reza Hajipour <rehaj...@gmail.com>
> > > > > > > > wrote:
> > > > > > > > > sum-to-zero constraints ensure the identifiability, if yes, is
> > > > > > > > > it
> > > > > > > > > necessary to have this constraint on 'iid' parts, as follows?
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > formula <- O ~ X +
> > > > > > > > >   f(ID.area, model="besag", graph=.... , constr=TRUE) +
> > > > > > > > >   f(ID.area1, model="iid", constr=TRUE) +
> > > > > > > > >   f(ID.year, model="rw2", constr=TRUE) +
> > > > > > > > >   f(ID.year1, model="iid", constr=TRUE)
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > As you mentioned the constr=TRUE is default, if I don't add it
> > > > > > > > > to
> > > > > > > > > f(...) parts of the above formula, the conster is True and the
> > > > > > > > > sum-to-zero constraint is done for all random effects?
> > > > > > > > > On Saturday 2 March 2024 at 19:04:36 UTC+3:30 Helpdesk
> > > > > > > > > (Haavard
> > > > > > > > > Rue) wrote:
> > > > > > > > > >

> > > > > > > > > > 'besag'
> > > > > > > > > > part of the model, not the 'iid'

> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > On Sat, 2024-03-02 at 07:13 -0800, Reza Hajipour wrote:

> > > > > > > > > > > Thank you.
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > What about the "BYM" model where we have two random

> > > > > > > > > > > one with
> > > > > > > > > > > ICAR prior and one with gaussian prior, does it give sum-

> > > > > > > > > > > zero as
> > > > > > > > > > > follows:
> > > > > > > > > > >

> > > > > > > > > > > rankdef=1)
> > > > > > > > > > > On Saturday 2 March 2024 at 13:04:09 UTC+3:30 Helpdesk
> > > > > > > > > > > (Haavard Rue)
> > > > > > > > > > > wrote:
> > > > > > > > > > > > yes, this gives a sum-to-zero constraint. for the besag

> > > > > > > > > > > > On Fri, 2024-03-01 at 22:02 -0800, Reza Hajipour wrote:

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Re: diagonal argument in INLA control
messages.body_plain:
I'm not sure where you got the impression that it "speeds up" the inference. If things finish faster with that option, it will only be because the modified model is easier than the original, intended, model. In some cases, it can be used _very carefully_ to solve the original model, E.g. in a sequence of runs with gradually decreasing "diagonal" value. It does change the inference, so should not be used without proper consideration.

As the documentation says, this is an Expert option only, and it shouldn't be used if you don't understand the implications.

Finn

messages.subject: Increasing Influence of Spatial Effect
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am building a spatial-temporal binomial model looking at US counties - I have some counties with very rich data (lots of tests) and some data for very sparse data (few tests), so I am using INLA so that we can impute missing values in counties with sparse data (i.e., we are modeling the proportion of positive tests over total tests).

The ideal model performance is that in counties with rich data, the model returns (predicts) the rich data back (i.e., with little to no change) and that in counties with sparser data, the model offers an imputation that takes into account the neighboring counties rates.

Currently, I have landed on a Knorr-Held type-model of the form:

OUTCOME ~ 1 + f(MONTH, model = "iid") + f(COUNTY, model = "iid") + f(COUNTY2, model = "besag", graph = mat, group = MONTH2, control.group = list(model = "rw1"))

Where we have random effects for both time and space and an interaction between space (as a besag) and time (rw1)

This model does almost everything that I want it to, with one issue: I cannot really seem to get neighboring counties with sparse data to be influenced by their neighbors with rich data. Instead, the overall average of the entire dataset (informed by the temporal random effect) is what appears to primarily inform the imputation/prediction.

So, my question is, are there any recommendations for improving the strength of the spatial effect of the model so that neighbors with sparse data are more strongly influenced by neighbors with rich data? I have searched for tutorials but have unfortunately not found what I am looking for.

Any assistance or pointing me towards resource to better inform myself how I can do this would be appreciated. Thank you!

Charles

Thank you.

I fitted the spatio-temporal interaction model using this code

st2<- O ~ 1+f(ID.city,model=“bym”,graph=g,scale.model = T,constr=T,hyper=pc1)+
  f(ID.year,model=“ar1”,hyper=pc2,constr=T)+
  f(ID.year1, model = “iid”,hyper=pc2,constr=T)+

  f(ID.city1, model=“iid”,hyper=pc2,constr=T,group=ID.year2,control.group = list(model=“ar1”))

 The spatio-temporal interaction effects extracted from this are consistent with “time-varying”, but I can't extract the correct temporal and spatial effects

I use generic0 to impose constraints on the spatio-temporal interaction terms
st3<- O ~ 1+f(ID.city,model=“bym”,graph=g,scale.model = T,constr=T,hyper=pc1)+

  f(ID.year,model=“ar1”,hyper=pc2,constr=T)+
  f(ID.year1, model = “iid”,hyper=pc2,constr=T)+

  f(cityyear,model=“generic0”, Cmatrix=R2, rankdef=rank.def2,
    constr=TRUE, hyper=list(prec=list(prior=pc2)),
    extraconstr=list(A=A.constr2, e=e2)
  )

I can extract the correct time and space effects from this, but the spatio-temporal interaction effects do not match the “time change”

How can I do this?

> > > > > > > > or
> > > > > > > > not?
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > On Thursday 7 March 2024 at 09:59:30 UTC+3:30 Elias T. Krainski
> > > > > > > > wrote:
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > Hi,
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > You do not always need constr = TRUE. It is not needed for 'iid'
> > > > > > > > > model, or any other model with proper joint distribution. But
> > > > > > > > > sometimes you want it, for example for the case of having a long
> > > > > > > > > range correlation that interacts with some other model
> > > > > > > > > component.
> > > > > > > > > You only need constraint in intrinsic models if another model
> > > > > > > > > component includes its null space.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > Please take a look at the example below, where I illustrate the
> > > > > > > > > fact
> > > > > > > > > that you do not always need to add a constraint while working
> > > > > > > > > with
> > > > > > > > > intrinsic models.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > library(INLA)
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > n <- 30
> > > > > > > > > x <- scale(cumsum(rnorm(n)))
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > plot(x)
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > y <- rpois(n, exp(2 + x))
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > fit1 <- inla(
> > > > > > > > >     y ~ f(i, model = 'rw1'),
> > > > > > > > >     data = list(i = 1:n, y = y),
> > > > > > > > >     family = 'poisson'
> > > > > > > > > )
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > ## The intercept captures the overall mean
> > > > > > > > > fit1$summary.fix
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > ## posterior mean for the constrained random effect is around
> > > > > > > > > zero
> > > > > > > > > summary(fit1$summary.random$i$mean)
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > ## Now, take the intercept ou of the linear predictor
> > > > > > > > > ## Then, the constraint in the random effect is no longer needed
> > > > > > > > > fit2 <- inla(
> > > > > > > > >     y ~ 0 + f(i, model = 'rw1', constr = FALSE),
> > > > > > > > >     data = list(i = 1:n, y = y),
> > > > > > > > >     family = 'poisson'
> > > > > > > > > )
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > ## unconstrained random effect is around the intercept (not
> > > > > > > > > fitted
> > > > > > > > > separately)
> > > > > > > > > summary(fit2$summary.random$i$mean)
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > ## However, the fitted values are similar (not exactly the same
> > > > > > > > > as
> > > > > > > > > the priors are different and there are some small numerical
> > > > > > > > > differences while doing the computations)
> > > > > > > > > summary(fit1$summary.fitted.values$mean)
> > > > > > > > > summary(fit2$summary.fitted.values$mean)
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > regards,
> > > > > > > > > Elias

messages.body_plain:
The correct solution depends on how you’ve defined the observation  models, specifically the prediction formula(s).
What fmesher and inlabru versions do you have? If it’s too old you would need to explicitly tell like() what components are involved, so it can avoid evaluation it. The latest version detects it automatically.
However, the error says that _all_ the evaluations gave NULL, indicating a bug in your code. Check what each of your eval.* functions return when given your different point data, and when given the integration points. If you have a special variable in the data telling the functions what to return, it needs to be present in the integration data. This should be doable by having it in the “samplers” input.
Finn

> On 19 May 2024, at 13:29, kyriakos nikolaou <kyria...@gmail.com> wrote:
>

> ﻿Hello,
>
> Related on my last question, as I said I wanted to fit an LGCP on multiple realizations, so I followed your suggestion, to stich the point patterns next to each other but keeping them disconnected. I did the same thing for their corresponding fixed effects so in the end I had a spatial pixels data frame where the fixed effects where one next to each other and spaced by a certain margin that evaluates to zero.
>
> Now, I wanted to keep everything like this but have an independent intercept for each realization. Therefore I followed a similar tactic of constructing spatial pixel data frames that are one on their corresponding realization and zero on the others. so my full model would look like this
>
> # full model idepedent intercept
> model.full <- coordinates ~
>   field(coordinates,model = spde) +
>   BE(eval.BE(.data.), model = "linear") +
>   PM(eval.PM(.data.), model = "linear") +
>   BM(eval.BM(.data.), model = "linear") +
>   I1(eval.I1(.data.), model = "linear") +
>   I2(eval.I2(.data.), model = "linear") +
>   I3(eval.I3(.data.), model = "linear") +
>   I4(eval.I4(.data.), model = "linear") +
>   I5(eval.I5(.data.), model = "linear") +
>   I6(eval.I6(.data.), model = "linear")
>
> However inlabru realized im trying to construct intercepts but it wants me to follow its own way of doing it as I understand, here is the error
>
> Warning in add_mapper(component$main, label = component$label, lhoods = lh, : All covariate evaluations for 'I1' are NULL; an intercept component was likely intended. Implicit latent intercept component specification is deprecated since version 2.1.14.
> Use explicit notation '+ I1(1)' instead.
>
> following its notation means I have a global intercept, which is not what i want. Is there a way around this?
>
> Thank you,
> Kyriacos

>

> > > ﻿
> > > ﻿Hi,
> > > This is an interesting case.
> > >
> > > For the SPDE, one option is if you can make a joint mesh instead of having them as separate meshes. They don’t need to be geographically connected. As long as they are part of the same mesh object and the regions don’t overlap, you’ll get the effect you describe, where it’s the same SPDE model for all the regions.
> > >
> > > For the covariate, your can let your f.DM() function take an additional argument with a vector that says which “covariate map” to apply. Or an argument with a scalar that says what to do, and use the _eval feature in the predictor, like this:
> > > Form1 <- DM_eval(f.DM(.data., 1)) + f
> > > Form2 <- DM_eval(f.DM(.data., 2)) + f
> > > etc.
> > > With that option, you can use different f.DM functions for each dataset as well. The component definition can be simply DM(1).
> > >
> > > Finn
> > >
> > > > On 12 May 2024, at 12:47, kyriakos nikolaou <kyria...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > >
> > > > ﻿Hello,
> > > >
> > > > I am trying to fit a LGCP model for which I have a Matern field and a spatial covariate in inlabru, this is how I construct the model and run the  inference for a single data set
> > > >
> > > > spde <- inla.spde2.pcmatern(mesh = mesh, prior.range = c(1, 0.01),  prior.sigma = c(3.0, 0.01))
> > > >
> > > > model <- coordinates ~ DM(f.DM(.data.), model = "linear") +  f(coordinates, model = spde) +     Intercept(1)
> > > >
> > > > fit <- inlabru::lgcp(components=model, data=spdf.pp, samplers = sampler.spdf , domain = list(coordinates = mesh))
> > > >
> > > > However, I have multiple datasets (set of points and covariate map and a different study region) and I want to fit them to the model assuming they are generated from the same process. Therefore, I want a posterior distribution for the range, sigma, the coefficient of the covariate and the intercept using all the data.
> > > >
> > > >  I believe this has to to do with the Multiple likelihoods, LGCPs - Multiple Likelihoods • inlabru (inlabru-org.github.io) <https://inlabru-org.github.io/inlabru/articles/2d_lgcp_multilikelihood.html>, however I am really lost in implementing as in my case I have different mesh, and a different covariate map for each data set.
> > > >
> > > > Could you help me out on how I could translate the above piece of code into one that takes into account multiple datasets ( set of points, covariates, regions/mesh)?

> > > > Thank you in advance, best regards,

messages.subject: Runtimes slower this year than last
messages.subject_clean: Runtimes slower this year than last
messages.body_plain:
It's so cool to see so many people using INLA. I remember reading the GMRF book probably about 20 years ago and playing around with some models. I'm finally using it for a pretty big project. I had a student run INLA last year and it took 36 hours to complete a multivariate spatio-temporal model, 3000 spatial points, 20 time points, 20 age groups with some random covariate effects and some spatially varying random covariate effects. I run it now and it's been going for about 3 weeks with no end in sight. I'm curious if the change in Pardiso licensing could be to blame. Is there any other reason I would be seeing that and any other way to get that initial speed back? Here is the heart of the code I'm running:

# create the linear combination for the temporal effects

temporal_lcs <- inla.make.lincombs(year_id = diag(18), year_id2 = diag(18))

names(temporal_lcs) <- c("2000", "2001", "2002", "2003", "2004", "2005", "2006", "2007", "2008", "2009",

                         "2010", "2011", "2012", "2013", "2014", "2015", "2016", "2017")

# create the linear combination for the age effects

age_lcs <- inla.make.lincombs(age_id = diag(18), age_id2 = diag(18))

names(age_lcs) <- c("ag1", "ag2", "ag3", "ag4", "ag5", "ag6", "ag7", "ag8", "ag9", "ag10",

                    "ag11", "ag12", "ag13", "ag14", "ag15", "ag16", "ag17", "ag18")

# combine the lincear combinations

all_lcs <- c(temporal_lcs, age_lcs)

# specify the model formula

formula <- Freq ~ 1 + # intercept

                  f(num, model = "iid", diagonal = 1e-3, constr = TRUE)  + # iid effect

                  f(year_id, model = "rw1", scale.model = TRUE, diagonal = 1e-3, constr = TRUE) + # structured temporal effect

                  f(year_id2, model = "iid", diagonal = 1e-3, constr = TRUE) + # iid temporal effect

                  f(county_id, model = "bym", graph = W, scale.model = TRUE, diagonal = 1e-3, constr = TRUE) + # county effect

                  f(age_id, model = "rw1", scale.model = TRUE, diagonal = 1e-3, constr = TRUE) + # structured age group effect

                  f(age_id2, model = "iid", diagonal = 1e-3, constr = TRUE) + # iid age

                  f(edu_id, model = "dmatern", locations = edu_values, constr = TRUE) + # education effect

                  f(hhsize_id, model = "dmatern", locations = hhsize_values, constr = TRUE) + # household size effect

                  f(mar_id, model = "dmatern", locations = mar_values, constr = TRUE) + # marital status effect

                  f(unemp_id, model = "dmatern", locations = unemp_values, constr = TRUE) + # unemployment rate effect

                  f(homevalue_id, model = "dmatern", locations = homevalue_values, constr = TRUE) + # homevalue effect

                  f(race_id, model = "dmatern", locations = race_values, constr = TRUE) + # race effect

                  f(unemp_id2, model = "dmatern", locations = unemp_values, constr = TRUE, group = state_id, control.group = list(model = "besag", graph = StateW)) + # race interaction effect

                 f(homevalue_id2, model = "dmatern", locations = homevalue_values, constr = TRUE, group = state_id2, control.group = list(model = "besag", graph = StateW)) + # homevalue interaction effect

                  f(race_id2, model = "dmatern", locations = race_values, constr = TRUE, group = state_id3, control.group = list(model = "besag", graph = StateW))  # unemployment interaction effect

## Fit and Save Female Model

fmodel1 <- inla(formula, family = "binomial", data = fdata, Ntrials = pop, control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE, link = 1), control.compute = list(dic = TRUE),

                control.inla = list(strategy = "adaptive", int.strategy = "eb"), num.threads = "30:-2", control.fixed=list(prec.intercept=1), inla.mode = "experimental",lincomb = all_lcs,safe = TRUE)

save(fmodel1, file = "fmodel1.Rdata")

I have also tried a few other options, like safe = FALSE, switching out some matern covariances for ar1 structures, strategy = gaussian, for example. I haven't come close to exhausting every optional argument I'm sure, but I've played around a bit with it.

messages.body_plain:
a loggamma(a,b) prior for theta = "log precision", is the same as a Gamma(a,b)
prior for the precision (where E() = a/b).

you normally do not need to change the initial value, as its better for the
optimizer to have a to tight model adapting to data than the other way around.

setting fixed=TRUE, simply treat theta=log(10) as a constant, I guess this is
not what you want.

messages.subject: Error running new model with a spatial spde effect
messages.subject_clean: Error running new model with a spatial spde effect
messages.body_plain:
Hi INLA team
I have not used INLA for about a year and it seems some things have changed related to mesh construction. I am using it for a new project and have recently installed it on my new computer so I am not sure how much either of those is having an effect.

when I run the model without the spde spatial effect it runs fine but when I add the spde model I get an error message if anyone knows what this might be referring to:

Error in !is.null(h) && !is.null(h[[key]]) && !(is.na <http://is.na>(h[[key]])) : 'length = 3' in coercion to 'logical(1)'

A<-fm_basis(mesh, loc=Loc1)

spde2 <- INLA::inla.spde2.pcmatern(mesh,
                             prior.range = c(3, 0.05),
                             prior.sigma = c(1, 0.05))

w2.index <- inla.spde.make.index(name = 'w',
                                 n.spde = spde2$n.spde)

Stack2 <- inla.stack(
  tag = "Fit",
  data = list(waterTempMax = MYM$waterTempMax),
  A = list(1, A),
  effects = list(
    data=covs,
    w  = w2.index))

f1.lm <- waterTempMax ~ -1 + intercept + airTempMax + CatchArea + Riparian + f(w, model = spde2)

I1.lm <- inla(f1.lm,
              family = "gaussian",
              data = inla.stack.data(Stack2),
              control.fixed = list(prec=1,
                               prec.intercept=1),
              control.compute = list(dic = TRUE),
              control.predictor = list(A = inla.stack.A(Stack2),
                                       compute = TRUE, #
                                       link = 1),
              control.inla=list(int.strategy = 'eb'),
              verbose=T)

messages.subject: Scale.model option in inla
messages.body_plain:
Hi INLA Members,

I have a question regarding scale.mode. I see that

scale.model

Logical. If TRUE then scale the RW1 and RW2 and BESAG and BYM and BESAG2 and RW2D models so the their (generlized) variance is 1. Default value is inla.getOption("scale.model.default")

Now, say if I use my model,

Y`X+f(ID,X,model="besag")

In that case If I use scale.model=T, will it resolve identifiability issue? If not how can we do so? (as it is a spatially varying coefficient part included, I keep const=F)

P.S.: Identifiability issue comes in my opinion as the model seems to be Y=intercept+X \beta_1 + X \beta_ID,X = intercept+X(\beta1+\beta_ID,X)

Alokesh.

>
> Hi J,
>
> I think the name 'values' is causing the confusion, as 'values' defined where
> the RW2 is defined, while the 'weights', ie your covariate values, goes into the
> 2nd unnamed argument.
>
> I would try with
>
>
> f(age_binyr_idx, cortisol_log, model = "rw2", constr=FALSE, scale.model = TRUE)
>
> normally, constr=F is required as you do not want the coefficients to sum to
> zero
>
> let me know
>
> H
>
>
> On Thu, 2024-03-28 at 13:26 -0700, Jessica Godwin wrote:
> > Hi,
> >
> > I know not having a reproducible example is bad form, but my data is not
> > shareable and I'm not entirely sure how to reproduce the bug.
> >
> > I have longitudinal data of cortisol and testosterone measures for individuals
> > going through puberty. Letting a represent age bin (a = 1 corresponds to [8,
> > 8.5), a = 2  is [8.5, 9), etc..), I want to fit the following model:
> >
> > test_{ai} | \eta_{ai}, \tau_y, \tau_{beta} \tau_{gamma} ~ N(\eta_{ai},
> > \tau_y^{-1})
> > \eta_{ia} = \alpha_a + \beta_a x cort_{ai} + \gamma_i
> > \beta_a ~ RW2(\tau_{beta})
> > \gamma_i ~ N(0, \tau_{gamma}^{-1})
> >
> > Where test_{ai} are log testosterone observations and cort_{ai} are log
> > cortisol observations for individual i at age group a, \alpha_a are age bin-
> > specific intercepts, \gamma_i are IID random intercepts for each individual,
> > and \beta_a are coefficients describing the linear relationship between
> > cortisol and testosterone for those in age bin a with a smoothing prior on
> > them.
> >
> > To specify this model I use the following formula and inla() call
> >
> > formula_HC <- testosterone_log ~ -1 + age_binyrhalf +
> > f(fieldcode,  model = "iid") +
> > f(age_binyr_idx, values = cortisol_log, model = "rw2", scale.model = TRUE)
> >
> > mod_HC <- inla(formula_HC, data = mod_data, family = "gaussian")
> >
> > where age_binyrhalf is a factor variable with my age groups, field code is a
> > character variable with unique individual identifiers, and age_binyr_idx is a
> > numeric vector with values 1, 2, etc. corresponding to the numeric levels
> > associated with the categorial labels of age_binyrhalf.
> >
> > The issue is when I try to run this, I get an error that The 'values' given in
> > f(age_binyr_idx, ..., values=) are not unique, it tells me I have 440 unique
> > values instead of 446. (Attaching a screenshot of the output). However, tests
> > of equality/tables, etc of my values show I have 446 unique values. I suspect
> > this is maybe due to some rounding issues within INLA.
> >
> > Can anyone help me with this issue?
> >
> > Thank you! And, sorry again, that I cannot reproduce this issue with simulated
> > data (I tried!)
> >
> > All the best,
> > Jessica Godwin

Hello,
I am running a nonstationary INLA model, with varying kappa. I ran the model on my laptop with only three columns in B.kappa and B.tau in order to test whether it worked, and I had no trouble.  But I tried to run the model with full B matrices and I got a crash saying Error with INLA : Condition `nfactors >= nfac_from && nfactors <= nfac_to' is not TRUE. I have run models with nonstationary kappa on the same cluster before without trouble. Does this message seem familiar to you ?
Thanks to you all, as ususal
Sébastien

messages.subject: Trying to sample from posterior with RW and other random effects
messages.subject_clean: Trying to sample from posterior with RW and other random effects
messages.body_plain:
Hi INLA discussion forum. I am working on a thesis project and trying to sample from the posterior of my distribution to determine if the model I selected is correct (also might be nice for simulation down the road). For a little context this is a spatiotemporal model that needs to account for both spatial clustering (included a besag term), as well as variation in both space and time for my spatial units (included RW(1) with a replicate on my state variable for time).

I am just making sure that I've checked all of the boxes I need to before I defend my choices in a few weeks. So, I am trying to determine if the number of zeros produced by my model warrants the use of the zeroinflated models offered by INLA, but I am a little confused. First, I'm just generally unsure if I'm doing this correctly (code below). More to the point, I'm confused as to why I get estimates for every all time points in my RW(1) term. I would think I would get t-1 terms since t2 is conditional on t1. So there's obviously one or more things I'm not understanding if I'm getting RW estimates for the first point in my time series.

# number of simulations to generate sims
nsims <- 100
# vector to hold number of zeros produced by model
nzeros <- c()
for(l in 1:nsims){
posterior.samples<-inla.posterior.sample(n=1, out.negbin.dat)
  # grab posterior estimates for fixed effects
  # overall intercept
  intercept<-posterior.samples[[1]]$latent["(Intercept):1",1][[1]]
  prop.M<-posterior.samples[[1]]$latent['scale(prop.M):1',1][[1]]
  min.cv.fd<-posterior.samples[[1]]$latent['scale(min.cv.fd):1',1][[1]]
  wsi <- posterior.samples[[1]]$latent['scale(wsi.ttl):1',1][[1]]

  # random effects
  # this will get the RW(1) predictors for all years
  # rw.terms are random walk of order 1
  rw.terms<-unlist(lapply(posterior.samples, function(s) s$latent[paste0("idarea2:", seq(1,
                                                                                    n_distinct(WIDat.hunt.y$uid)*n_distinct(WIDat.hunt.y$year),1)), 1]))
  # besag ests
  besag.terms<-unlist(lapply(posterior.samples, function(s) s$latent[paste0("idarea:", seq(1,
                                                                                    n_distinct(WIDat.hunt.y$uid),1)), 1]))
  # iid intercepts
  iid.terms<-unlist(lapply(posterior.samples, function(s) s$latent[paste0("idarea4:", seq(1,
                                                                                    n_distinct(WIDat.hunt.y$uid),1)), 1]))
  # hyper pars
  hyperpars <- inla.hyperpar.sample(1, out.negbin.dat)
  size <- hyperpars[1] # overdispersion parm
  prec.besag <- hyperpars[2] # besag proc
  prec.rw <http://prec.rw> <- hyperpars[3] # rw proc
  prec.iid <- hyperpars[4] # iid
  nyear<-n_distinct(WIDat.hunt.y$year)
  nuid<-n_distinct(WIDat.hunt.y$uid)

  k<-1
  new.y <- c()
  for(i in 1:nyear){
    for(j in 1:nuid){
    mu<- WIDat.hunt.y$nSamp[((i-1)*nuid)+j]*exp(intercept + prop.M*scale(WIDat.hunt.y$prop.M)[[((i-1)*nuid)+j]] + wsi*scale(WIDat.hunt.y$wsi.ttl)[[((i-1)*nuid)+j]] + min.cv.fd*scale(WIDat.hunt.y$min.cv.fd)[[((i-1)*nuid)+j]] + rnorm(1, rw.terms[((i-1)*nuid)+j][[1]], 1/prec.rw <http://prec.rw>) + rnorm(1,besag.terms[j][[1]], 1/prec.besag) + rnorm(1,iid.terms[j][[1]], 1/prec.iid))
    new.y[k] <- rnbinom(n=1, mu=mu, size=size)
    k <- k + 1
      }
    }
  nzeros[l] <- length(which((new.y==0)))
}

messages.body_plain:
The internal representation of a density in INLA does not know that x > 0, say,
hence if

	z ~ normal

and

	x <- exp(z)

then, there can be small prob for x < 0, due to this. a you guess, the more x is
concentrated close to zero, this can happen.

This is mainly an issue for the 'fitted.values', which you can control yourself
from the linear predictor and compute properties wrt 'z' above, instead of 'x'.

like

	E(x) = int f_x(x) * x dx = int f_z(z) * exp(z) dz

where the 'z' representation will not have this issue that 'exp(z)' could be
negative.

it could also be for the hyperparameters, where you can find the hyperparameter
in its internal representation in `internal', like

> r=inla(y~1,data=data.frame(y=0))
> r$internal.marginals.hyperpar[[1]]
                 x               y
 [1,]  4.749390900 0.0019227601837
 [2,]  4.951068336 0.0053327403227

messages.subject: Plotting spatial effect
messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA community.

I am interested in plotting the spatial effect of the INLA model, the code I am using is this, to obtain the mean and the standard deviation of the spatial effect and for plotting it.

mean_s <- inla.mesh.project(proj, res$summary.random$s$mean)
sd_s <- inla.mesh.project(proj, res$summary.random$s$sd)

gmean <- ggplot(df, aes(x = x, y = y, fill = mean_s)) + geom_raster() +
  scale_fill_viridis(name = "Mean Spatial Effect", na.value = "transparent",
                     option = "inferno") +
  coord_fixed(ratio = 1) + theme_bw()

And it works but for other purposes I am interested in obtaining that spatial effect in each point, like one usually obtain the predictions of the model on each point. The problem is tha I that those function make a projection using the mesh so I would that it is not that directly, but is there any way to do this? I am familiar that there some more updated version using fmesher but the problem is the same with this.

Does anyone have any idea how to do this?

Thank you for your help.

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Plotting spatial effect
messages.body_plain:
As the spde model represents a continuous field yes you can project the field at any location. Because it is discretized (in inla using a mesh) the projection is from the discretized locations. Therefore in inla you always do it from the mesh. All you need to do is to build a 'proj' object to project for the locations you want. To do this for the observed locations, you can do A %*% res$summary.random$s$mean (where A is the projector you used to fit the model).
There are examples in Chapter 2 of https://becarioprecario.bitbucket.io/spde-gitbook/

messages.subject: Modelling with NA's in covariates
messages.body_plain:
Hi everybody,

I want to set up a spatio-temporal model for the length of dry spells over lets say 2001-2005.
I want to use the following covariates: elevation, Dry_week, temp_min, temp_max, temp_mean and pressure_mean, which means my model should look like this:

Length_dry_spell~-1+Intercept+Elevation+Dry_week+Temp_mean+Temp_min+Temp_max+spatio-temporal field.

However, for some weeks the covariates  Dry_week, temp_min, temp_max, temp_mean and pressure_mean are NA's. Where Dry_week is either TRUE, FALSE or NA.

Does that mean that firstly I have to build a model Temp_mean~-1+Intercept+Elevation +spatio-temporal field
Then secondly Temp_min ~-1+Intercept+Elevation+Temp_mean+spatio-temporal field
Thirdly Temp_max~-1+Intercept+Elevation+Temp_mean+Temp_min+spatio-temporal field
And so on... Or is there a different way for doing? And how do I include Dry_week. Is it appropriate if it is a factor?

Best and thanks in advance,
Corinna

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Plotting spatial effect
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

in addition to Elias' reply (which mostly describes what goes on
inside inla.mesh.project()), it's not entirely clear what you're
asking for.
Like Elias, said, the spde/mesh models define the field continuously
through space, so there's no such thing as evaluating it at "each
point", as those are infinitely many. The best one can do is evaluate
it at locations of interest; the default fm_evaluate() and
fm_evaluator() functions (formerly
inla.mesh.project()/inla.mesh.projector()) constructs a lattice that's
handy for lotting, but you can supply locations of your own choice
instead. At the heart of the calculations is the fm_basis() function,
that computes the A matrix Elias mentioned, such that A %*%
coefficients evaluates the field at given locations, when
"coefficients" are weights for the mesh basis functions (such as the
$summary.random$...$mean and $sd values).

I would recommend reading the details of the ?fm_evaluate
documentation, in particular for fm_evaluator(), that takes a mesh
argument and a loc argument, where loc defines the points where the
field should be evaluated.
The fm_evaluator() method can be used to speed up repeated
fm_evaluate() calls for the same set of locations, so it only needs to
evaluate the A matrix once.

The added benefit of using fm_evaluate/or() instead of manual A <-
fm_basis(...) calls is that the evaluator methods keep track of if
some points were outside of the mesh, so it can assign NA to such
evaluations. The A matrix rows corresponding to such points will
simply be all-zero, which isn't usually what one wants to get for
missing/invalid data; NAs can be handled correctly by e.g. plotting
methods.

Finn

messages.subject: Overfitting in Spatiotemporal models
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am trying to fit a spatiotemporal model for diabetes cases in Cape Town for my Thesis. The models I have fitted were adapted from Blangiardo et al (2013) paper"Spatial and spatio-temporal models with R-INLA" and her textbook. The models are namely a "Non parametric dynamic trend" and a "Type 1 interaction" model. The issue I am having is with both models, the estimated relative risks are so close to calculated standardized incidence ratios that they are almost indistinguishable (within three decimal places of each other).I believe something is causing the model to overfit but I can't figure out what.

 Interestingly, I fit a 3rd model that doesn't have this issue. For this third model I only fit the structured time effect as "iid" and it give desired results. The issue with the models remain the same whether fixed effects (or covariates) are included or not.

To help understand my issue, I attached a slimmed down, simple reproducible example of my code. Your help would be greatly appreciated.

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

Thank you very much for your answer to my previous questions.

I have real datas and really wish to obtains maps from them and the predictions from INLA.
Can I use the fitted.Predictor given by bru to obtain a maps as follow ?
# get easting and northing limits
bbox <- fm_bbox(hull[[1]])
grd_dims <- round(c(x = diff(bbox[[1]]), y = diff(bbox[[2]])) / 2000)

# make mesh projector to get model summaries from the mesh to the mapping grid
mesh_proj <- fm_evaluator(
new_mesh,
xlim = c(100000, 1400000), ylim = c(5900000, 7150000), dims = grd_dims
)

# make a terra raster stack with the posterior median and range95
make_terra_raster_stack <- function(pred_grids) {
out_stk <- rast()

for (j in 1:1) {
mean_j <- cbind(expand.grid(x = mesh_proj$x, y = mesh_proj$y),
Z = c(matrix(pred_grids[[j]][, 1], grd_dims[1]))
)
mean_j <- rast(mean_j, crs = "EPSG:2154")
range95_j <- cbind(expand.grid(X = mesh_proj$x, Y = mesh_proj$y),
Z = c(matrix(pred_grids[[j]][, 2], grd_dims[1]))
)
range95_j <- rast(range95_j, crs = "EPSG:2154")
out_j <- c(mean_j, range95_j)
terra::add(out_stk) <- out_j
}
names(out_stk) <- c(
"u_median", "u_range95"
)
out_stk <- terra::crop(out_stk, states, mask = TRUE)
return(out_stk)
}

make_plot_field <- function(data_stk, scale_label, title) {
ggplot(states) +
geom_sf(fill = NA) +
coord_sf(datum = NA) +
geom_spatraster(data = data_stk) +
labs(x = "", y = "") +
scale_fill_distiller(scale_label,
palette = "Spectral",
na.value = "transparent"
) +
theme_bw() +
ggtitle(title) +
geom_sf(fill = NA)
}

pred <- data.frame(
median = exp(res_svc_plus$summary.fitted.values[446:4017,"0.5quant"]),
range95 = exp(res_svc_plus$summary.fitted.values[446:4017,"0.975quant"]) -
exp(res_svc_plus$summary.fitted.values[446:4017,"0.025quant"])
)

pred_grids <- lapply(
list(pred = pred),
function(x) as.matrix(fm_evaluate(mesh_proj, x))
)

out_stk <- make_terra_raster_stack(pred_grids = pred_grids)
plot_pred_median <- make_plot_field(
data_stk = out_stk[["u_median"]],
scale_label = "posterior\nmedian\nCd_mousse_s",
title
)

Best regards,
Alizée

Le vendredi 26 avril 2024 à 17:53:02 UTC+2, Finn Lindgren a écrit :
> Hi,
>
> the way you defined the components, the X values at the observation
> locations need to be provided in the input data. Your model definition
> links each X=value to a corresponding observation, without involving
> space at all, so it will use the appropriate values and doesn't
> involve the mesh. The mesh is only involved when evaluating the
> u-component.
>
> In your predict() call, you've only provided locations, but no X
> values. Add the X-values for the fm_pixels() locations to the newdata
> input and it should work; you need newdata to have the same
> information about model inputs as your original estimation data
> (except the response variable which isn't needed/used).
>
> If you want X to be evaluated automatically (e.g. from a raster) based
> on the locations/geometry, you need to redefine the X-component to
> take the raster as input, so inlabru can evaluate it at the given
> prediction locations.
> (alternatively, use X_eval(eval_spatial(the_raster, .data.)) instead
> of X in the prediction expression).

messages.body_plain:
This relies on the details of how you’ve specified the input data and predictor expression in the model estimation; if possible, don’t rely on the hardcoded indexing into fitted.values (it looks like it assumes the specific fitted.values correspond to the field values at the mesh nodes perhaps?), but rather extract the relevant rows by name or similar (or saved information based on how you specified your input data). Otherwise it looks plausible, if you’re extracting the correct information from fitted.values (which may or may not be true, depending on how you setup the model).
Like I said in my previous reply, I would do this with predict() instead.
Finn

messages.subject: Model Selection when there is an Spatial Component
messages.subject_clean: Model Selection when there is an Spatial Component
messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA community

I am working on a spatial model using INLA and I have already fitted the model and now I want to do a model selection to decide between two likelihood (and also a variable selection for the model) however the usual metrics does not seem to work in this case where there is an spatial component.

Usually one would use the DIC, WAIC and CPO however when you have an spatial component the WAIC and CPO (which is basically a cross-validation Leave One Out) do not work because the split the data or the point does not take on accoun the spatial structure of the data. And with the DIC if the mean of the posterior does not summarize good enought the posterior distirbution is not usually a good measure (I am workin with a normal and lognormal likelihood so I think that maybe in this situation the DIC would be a good measure but I am not sure)

So does anyone know in this case what could be a better to do a variable selection and a comparision between different models when some models have a normal likelihood and others a lognormal likelihood?

messages.subject: First-Difference Correlated Random Walk for "Animal Movement"
messages.subject_clean: First-Difference Correlated Random Walk for "Animal Movement"
messages.body_plain:
Hi INLA team,

I'm trying to set up a 2-dimensional (longitude/latitude) state-space model that runs a first-difference correlated random walk that's commonly applied in animal movement studies (example paper: https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1890/04-1852 ) in the INLA framework.

This is for marine "animals" that cannot move across land, but it's not clear to me how I would implement the barrier meshes in this situation. I'm hopefully trying to reconstruct accurate daily positions of these "animals". Many of the coordinates of observations also have different levels of uncertainty (exact longitude coordinates are often missing and/or are much more uncertain that latitude coordinates are). The time variable is also expected to have some measurement error (probably gaussian and on the scale of hours). I also have strong prior beliefs that the process and observation models are very similar between different individuals, and therefore should be indexed hierarchically. This would especially be helpful for individuals where the number of observations/data quality is low.

There are helpful frequentist TMB-based packages for doing this type of modeling (see below), but these fit models independently for each individual, and can't handle missing longitude data or uncertainty in the time variable.
aniMotum: https://ianjonsen.github.io/aniMotum/index.html
crawl: https://github.com/NMML/crawl

How easy (if at all) would it be to cast these models into the INLA framework? Would a "rw2" model be close enough to a first-difference-correlated random walk to be useful? I've gone through the Ravishanker et al. "Dynamic time series models using R_INLA" book, but this doesn't seem to have quite what I'm looking for.

Kind regards,
Nick Freymueller

Dear INLA community,

I have a spatio-temporal INLA model where the covariates were standardized, because they are modelled with quadratic terms:

y ~ A + A² + B + B² + spde + AR(1)

My question is: if I want to make spatial predictions onto a raster, do the raster values need to be standardized as well, or can I use the raw (GIS) raster values?

Kind regards,
Charlotte Taelman

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Spatial predictions onto a raster with standardized covariates
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Spatial predictions onto a raster with standardized covariates
messages.body_plain:
Dear Charlotte,

You need to apply the _same_ standardisation to the covariate of the new data you want to use for prediction. Note that poly(x, 2) on the original dataset is most likely _not_ the same transformation as poly(x, 2) on the prediction dataset. Below is a small example. Note how the coefficients are different for the first two poly() calls. The last poly() has the same coefficients as the first.

covar <- iris$Sepal.Length
min(covar) |>
  seq(max(covar), length = 100) -> pred_covar
poly(covar, 2) |>
  attr("coefs")
poly(pred_covar, 2) |>
  attr("coefs")
poly(pred_covar, 2, coefs = attr(poly(covar, 2), "coefs"))

Best regards,

ir. Thierry Onkelinx

messages.subject_clean: CHANGE FROM GEOGRAPHICAL COORDINATES TO UTM COORDINATES IN AN INLA INTERPOLATION PERFORMED IN R
messages.body_plain:
I encounter a problem. In my script that works for R, to obtain an interpolation using INLA, when graphing the results the coordinates are geographical.It is worth mentioning that the coordinates of the excel and shape that I used in the script are found in UTM. I hope someone can help me. I need the coordinates to be passed to UTM. I share the script with whoever I work with. Greetings.
Script:
library(INLA)
library(readxl)
library(sp)
library(sf)
library(raster)
library(gstat)
library(tidyverse)
library(wesanderson)

lai_data <- read_excel("C:/Pro_R/Lai sin 0/BSD_CTD_CLSN_0.xlsx", sheet = "CL1")

SpatialPointsDataFrame
coordinates(lai_data) <- ~x+y

shape <- st_read("C:/Pro_R/Lai sin 0/Malla_Cl_1.shp")

mesh <- inla.mesh.2d(loc = coordinates(lai_data), max.edge = c(1, 5))

spde <- inla.spde2.matern(mesh = mesh, alpha = 2)

index <- inla.spde.make.index("spatial_field", spde$n.spde)

A_data <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh = mesh, loc = coordinates(lai_data))

stack_data <- inla.stack(
  data = list(y = lai_data$LAI),
  A = list(A_data, 1),
  effects = list(
    spatial_field = index,
    intercept = rep(1, nrow(lai_data))
  ),
  tag = "data"
)

formula <- y ~ 1 + f(spatial_field, model = spde)

result <- inla(
  formula,
  data = inla.stack.data(stack_data),
  family = "gaussian",
  control.predictor = list(A = inla.stack.A(stack_data), compute = TRUE),
  control.compute = list(dic = TRUE)
)

prediction_points <- st_make_grid(shape, cellsize = 1)

prediction_points_sp <- as(prediction_points, "Spatial")

A_pred <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh = mesh, loc = coordinates(prediction_points_sp))

stack_pred <- inla.stack(
  data = list(y = NA),
  A = list(A_pred, 1),
  effects = list(
    spatial_field = index,
    intercept = rep(1, length(prediction_points_sp))
  ),
  tag = "pred"
)

stack_full <- inla.stack(stack_data, stack_pred)

result_pred <- inla(
  formula,
  data = inla.stack.data(stack_full),
  family = "gaussian",
  control.predictor = list(A = inla.stack.A(stack_full), compute = TRUE),
  control.compute = list(dic = TRUE)
)

pred_index <- inla.stack.index(stack_full, "pred")$data
predictions <- result_pred$summary.fitted.values[pred_index, ]

print(head(predictions))

prediction_points <- st_as_sf(prediction_points)
prediction_points$LAI_pred <- predictions$mean Este no cargara si existe un numero diferente de filas, por lo que
se debera hacer acontinuacion esto antes y despues volver hacer estas lineas.

num_rows_points <- nrow(prediction_points)
print(num_rows_points)

num_rows_predictions <- nrow(predictions)
print(num_rows_predictions) #existe una diferiencia de una fila por lo que se debe corregir

if (num_rows_points > num_rows_predictions) {
  prediction_points <- prediction_points[1:num_rows_predictions, ]
} else if (num_rows_predictions > num_rows_points) {
  predictions <- predictions[1:num_rows_points, ]
}

prediction_points <- st_as_sf(prediction_points)
prediction_points$LAI_pred <- predictions$mean

if (st_crs(prediction_points) != st_crs(shape)) {
  shape <- st_transform(shape, st_crs(prediction_points))
}

prediction_points_clipped <- st_intersection(prediction_points, shape)

ggplot(prediction_points_clipped) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = LAI_pred)) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c() +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Interpolación de LAI usando INLA")
